tamil:
இரக்க இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின் கரப்பின்
அவர்பழி தம்பழி அன்று.
transliteration:
Irakka iraththakkaark kaanin karappin
avarpazhi thampazhi andru.
current_meaning: When you meet people it is fitting to ask, you may ask them; if they hide what they have and refuse, the blame is theirs, not yours.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you are really hungry and you politely ask a kind neighbour who has plenty of food for a little. If that neighbour pretends to have nothing, you did nothing wrong by asking. The person who hid the food is the one who acted badly.
university_explanation: The chapter on iravu (இரவு, 'asking, mendicancy') follows Nalkuravu (ch. 105, poverty) and is balanced by Iravachcham (ch. 107, dread of begging); together they permit asking only in real need and only of fitting givers. The key word irakka iraththakkaar (இரத்தக்கார், 'those of whom it is fit to ask') limits the permission: one may ask those able and willing to give. Karappin (கரப்பின், 'if they conceal') names the vice of hiding what one has, a word the chapter returns to again and again (karappu, karaththal); the commentarial line that follows Parimelazhagar, as reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, takes the blame (pazhi) as falling wholly on the one who conceals. Pope renders it 'Theirs is the sin, not yours, if they the gift deny.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல் இரந்தவை
துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்.
transliteration:
Inbam oruvarku iraththal irandhavai
thunbam uraaa varin.
current_meaning: Even asking can be a pleasure, if what is asked for comes without pain to either side.
elementary_explanation: If you ask a friend to share a crayon and they hand it over with a smile, asking feels nice, not embarrassing. Asking only hurts when the other person sighs or makes you feel small.
university_explanation: Valluvar makes the surprising claim that iraththal (இரத்தல், 'begging') can itself be inbam (இன்பம், 'pleasure'), on one condition: that what is begged comes thunbam uraaa (துன்பம் உறாஅ, 'without suffering'), where the lengthened uraaa is an alapedai (metrical lengthening). Commentators differ on whose suffering is meant: Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as the asker's (the gift comes without hardship), Solomon Pappaiah as the giver's reluctance, and Kalaignar as both minds, giver's and receiver's, being free of pain. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar stresses that the pleasure depends on the giver's goodwill (Puliyur Kesikan: ஈவாரது நல்லுணர்வால்). Pope: 'Even to ask an alms may pleasure give, / If what you ask without annoyance you receive.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று
இரப்புமோ ரேஎர் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Karappilaa nenjin kadanarivaar munnindru
irappumor eer udaiththu.
current_meaning: To stand before people whose hearts hide nothing and who know their duty, and ask of them, even that has a certain grace.
elementary_explanation: Asking your grandmother, who loves to share, for a slice of cake doesn't feel bad at all. It can even feel nice, because she is happy you asked.
university_explanation: Karappilaa nenju (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சு, 'a heart without concealment') and kadan arivaar (கடனறிவார், 'those who know their duty') describe the ideal giver. Kadan is read as duty (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah: 'this is my duty'), while Puliyur Kesikan glosses the givers as people who understand honour (மானம் அறிபவர்). The striking word is eer (ஏஎர், with alapedai lengthening, 'beauty, grace'): standing before such givers, even begging has beauty. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar reads the -um in irappum ('even begging') as conceding that begging is normally without grace. Pope: 'To stand as suppliants affords especial grace.' Texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, both printing the sandhi form இரப்புமோ ரேஎர்.

tamil:
இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும் கரத்தல்
கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Iraththalum eedhale polum karaththal
kanavilum thetraadhaar maattu.
current_meaning: Asking of people who would never think of withholding, even in a dream, is as honourable as giving.
elementary_explanation: Some people love sharing so much that when you ask them, it's like you're doing them a favour. With friends like that, asking feels almost as good as giving.
university_explanation: The line iraththalum eedhale polum (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும், 'begging too is just like giving') is one of the boldest claims in the Kural, and the emphatic ē in eedhale strengthens the equation. Its condition is that the giver karaththal kanavilum thetraadhaar (கரத்தல் கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார், 'does not know concealment even in a dream'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as conferring the same dignity (சிறப்பு, பெருமை) on such asking as on giving. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar explains the equation by the giver's joy: asking such a person gives him the chance to give. Pope: 'To beg of such ... is in fact the same as giving.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால் கண்ணின்று
இரப்பவர் மேற்கொள் வது.
transliteration:
Karappilaar vaiyagaththu unmaiyaal kannindru
irappavar merkol vadhu.
current_meaning: It is only because there are people in the world who never hold back that some take up asking, standing before others' eyes.
elementary_explanation: People bring their empty buckets to a well because they know the well has water. In the same way, people in need ask because they know there are kind people who will share.
university_explanation: The kural explains why anyone begs at all: because karappilaar (கரப்பிலார், 'those without concealment') exist in the world (vaiyagaththu unmaiyaal). Kan nindru (கண்ணின்று, 'standing before the eyes') is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as standing in front of a giver, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as asking with the eyes rather than with words, the silent request of the proud poor. Puliyur Kesikan adds that such people beg only to preserve life. The sense of merkolvadhu (மேற்கொள்வது, 'taking up' a practice) suggests begging chosen reluctantly because generous givers are known to exist. The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree (மேற்கொள் வது with a space in both).

tamil:
கரப்பிடும்பை யில்லாரைக் காணின் நிரப்பிடும்பை
எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்.
transliteration:
Karappidumbai yillaaraik kaanin nirappidumbai
ellaam orungu kedum.
current_meaning: At the mere sight of those free from the affliction of withholding, all the afflictions of want vanish at once.
elementary_explanation: When a hungry child sees a kind lunch lady who always shares, the worry disappears right away. Just seeing someone generous makes the scary feeling go.
university_explanation: The kural plays on two compounds built on idumbai (இடும்பை, 'affliction'): karappidumbai, the affliction (or 'disease', in Pappaiah's gloss நோய்) of concealment that belongs to the miser, and nirappidumbai, the affliction of want that belongs to the poor. The miser's karappu is thus treated as a sickness of its own, the counterpart of the beggar's poverty. Kaanin (காணின், 'if one but sees') shows that the mere sight of such a giver ends ellaam orungu (எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு, 'all together') the beggar's distress. Puliyur Kesikan adds that this holds for one who begs without losing self-respect (மானம் விடாமல்), and Kalaignar calls concealment an இழிநிலை (base state). The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, both printing the sandhi form யில்லாரைக்.

tamil:
இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவாரைக் காணின் மகிழ்ந்துள்ளம்
உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Igazhndhellaadhu eevaaraik kaanin magizhndhullam
ullul uvappadhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: When the asker meets givers who give without scorn or ridicule, his heart rejoices deep within.
elementary_explanation: If you ask for help and the person helps you with a kind smile instead of laughing at you, you feel warm and happy inside. How we give matters as much as what we give.
university_explanation: Igazhndhu ellaadhu (இகழ்ந்து எள்ளாது, 'without despising, without mocking') names the two insults a giver can add to a gift, contempt and derision; Pappaiah glosses them as அவமதிக்காமல், இழிவாகப் பேசாமல். The response is doubled for emphasis: magizhndhu (மகிழ்ந்து, 'rejoicing') and ullul uvappadhu (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது, 'delighting within the innermost heart'). The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar places the joy in the asker, and the next chapter, Iravachcham, will show the opposite case, where contempt makes asking unbearable. Pope: 'The minds of askers, through and through, will thrill with joy.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
இரப்பாரை இல்லாயின் ஈர்ங்கண்மா ஞாலம்
மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Irappaarai illaayin eerngkanmaa nyaalam
marappaavai sendruvan thatru.
current_meaning: If there were no askers, the comings and goings of this cool, wide world would be no more than wooden puppets moving to and fro.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a toy theatre where wooden puppets bounce around on strings. They move, but they don't really care about anything. Valluvar says that if no one ever needed help, people would be like those puppets, busy but with no kindness to show.
university_explanation: Eerngkanmaa nyaalam (ஈர்ங்கண்மா ஞாலம், 'the cool, wide, great earth') and marappaavai (மரப்பாவை, 'wooden doll') give the image: Mu. Varadarasanar explains it as a wooden puppet moved by strings, so that human activity without askers would be mechanical motion without inner meaning. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar takes the point to be that giving is what gives life its moral content, and giving needs askers. Kalaignar reads the couplet differently, making those who keep the poor at a distance no different from operated puppets. Pope: 'The mighty earth ... Will be a stage where wooden puppets come and go.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree (சென்றுவந் தற்று in both).

tamil:
ஈவார்கண் என்னுண்டாம் தோற்றம் இரந்துகோள்
மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை.
transliteration:
Eevaarkan ennundaam thotram irandhukol
mevaar ilaaak kadai.
current_meaning: What glory could givers have if there were no one who wished to ask and receive?
elementary_explanation: A goalkeeper can only be a hero if someone kicks the ball. In the same way, a generous person can only shine if someone needs their help.
university_explanation: Thotram (தோற்றம், 'appearance, eminence') is glossed as pugazh (புகழ், 'fame') by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar. Irandhu kol mevaar (இரந்துகோள் மேவார், 'those who wish to take by asking') are the counterpart without whom the giver's eminence cannot exist; ilaaak kadai has the alapedai lengthening ilaaa. Read with 1058, the couplet pair makes askers necessary to the moral economy of giving, a theme going back to Ch. 23 (Eegai) and Ch. 24 (Pugazh), where fame is linked to giving. Pope: 'What glory will there be to men of generous soul, / When none are found to love the askers' role?' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
இரப்பான் வெகுளாமை வேண்டும் நிரப்பிடும்பை
தானேயும் சாலும் கரி.
transliteration:
Irappaan vegulaamai vendum nirappidumbai
thaaneyum saalum kari.
current_meaning: One who asks must not grow angry when refused; his own distress of want is proof enough of how things stand.
elementary_explanation: If you ask a friend to share and they say no, don't get mad. You know how it feels not to have enough, so maybe they don't have enough either, or maybe it just wasn't the right time.
university_explanation: Vegulaamai (வெகுளாமை, 'not becoming angry') recalls Chapter 31 (Vegulaamai), here applied to the one who is refused. The second line is read in more than one way: nirappidumbai thaaneyum saalum kari (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி) can mean that the asker's own poverty is sufficient witness (kari, கரி) that things are not always available when wanted (Puliyur Kesikan, Pappaiah), that the asker's poverty teaches him (Mu. Varadarasanar), or that the refuser may be in the same plight as himself (Kalaignar). The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar takes the beggar's own want as reason enough for patience toward a refusal. Pope: 'Askers refused from wrath must stand aloof; / The plague of poverty itself is ample proof.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும்
இரவாமை கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Karavaadhu uvandheeyum kannannaar kannum
iravaamai koadi urum.
current_meaning: Even when there are people as dear as one's own eyes who would gladly give without hiding anything, not asking them at all is worth ten million times more.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your kindest aunt would happily give you anything you asked for. The Kural says it is still far better, and makes you stronger, to manage on your own and not ask, even from someone that kind.
university_explanation: The chapter Iravaccham (இரவச்சம், 'dread of begging') deliberately answers the preceding chapter Iravu (ch. 106), which permitted asking only of fitting, generous givers; here Valluvar raises the ideal higher, so that even such givers should not be asked. Karavaadhu (கரவாது, 'without concealing') and uvandhu eeyum (உவந்தீயும், 'who give with delight') describe the best possible donor, and kannannaar (கண்ணன்னார், 'those like one's eyes') marks them as most precious; the hyperbole koadi urum ('attains a crore', i.e. ten-million-fold good) is the commentators' measure of the superiority of not asking. In the line of interpretation that follows Parimelazhagar, as reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, the point is that dignity (maanam) lies in enduring want rather than in depending even on a willing friend. Pope renders it 'Ten million-fold 'tis greater gain, asking no alms to live, / Even from those, like eyes in worth, who nought concealing gladly give.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இரந்தும் உயிர்வாழ்தல் வேண்டின் பரந்து
கெடுக உலகியற்றி யான்.
transliteration:
Irandhum uyirvaazhdhal vendin parandhu
keduka ulagiyatri yaan.
current_meaning: If the one who shaped the world meant some people to live by begging, then let that maker himself wander about like a beggar and perish.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a game where the rules say some players must beg the others just to stay in. You would say the rules are unfair and the person who made them should try playing that way himself. That is how angry the Kural is that anyone should have to beg to live.
university_explanation: This is one of the boldest couplets in the Kural: Valluvar curses ulagiyatriyaan (உலகியற்றியான், 'he who fashioned the world') with the very fate of the beggar, parandhu keduga ('may he wander and perish'). Commentators in the tradition that follows Parimelazhagar read it as a conditional imprecation: if the creator had ordained begging as a means of life, he deserves to wander as beggars do; the force is ethical outrage that anyone should be reduced to irandhum ('even by begging') staying alive. Modern glosses differ in emphasis: Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the creator literal, while Kalaignar Karunanidhi's gloss pointedly says 'the one said to have created this world', distancing the verse from theism, and scholars have debated whether ulagiyatriyaan means a god, fate (ul), or the human order that permits destitution. Pope renders it 'If he that shaped the world desires that men should begging go, / Through life's long course, let him a wanderer be and perish so.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்துதீர் வாமென்னும்
வன்மையின் வன்பாட்ட தில்.
transliteration:
Inmai idumbai irandhudheer vaamennum
vanmaiyin vanpaatta thil.
current_meaning: There is no harder-hearted folly than the bold notion that the misery of poverty can be cured by begging instead of by effort.
elementary_explanation: If your bike breaks, you could keep asking friends to lend you theirs, or you could learn to fix your own. The Kural says choosing to ask forever instead of fixing things yourself is the worst choice of all.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on vanmai (வன்மை), 'hardness, toughness, boldness': the 'toughness' of deciding inmai idumbai (இன்மை இடும்பை, 'the affliction of want') will be ended by asking (irandhu theervaam) is called harder than any hardness (vanmaiyin vanpaattadhu il). Following Parimelazhagar's line, Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar supply the implied contrast with effort (muyarchi): the fault is abandoning work and choosing to live by others' gifts. Solomon Pappaiah adds the parenthesis '(without working it off)', and Pope's explanation speaks of remedying poverty 'by begging (rather than by working)'. Pope renders it 'Nothing is harder than the hardness that will say, / 'The plague of penury by asking alms we'll drive away'.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இடமெல்லாம் கொள்ளாத் தகைத்தே இடமில்லாக்
காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு.
transliteration:
Idamellaam kollaath thakaiththe idamillaak
kaalum iravollaach chaalbu.
current_meaning: The nobility that will not agree to beg even when one has nothing to live on is so great that the whole world cannot contain it.
elementary_explanation: Think of someone who has almost nothing but still won't ask for handouts, because they want to stand on their own feet. The Kural says that kind of courage is so big that even the whole world isn't big enough to hold it.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a pun on idam (இடம்): idamillaak kaalum means 'even when there is no means (of life)', while idamellaam kollaa means 'which all the room (of the world) cannot hold'. The quality praised is saalbu (சால்பு, 'nobility, fullness of character', the same root as saanraanmai, ch. 99), here specified as iravu ollaa, 'not consenting to beg'. In the line of commentary that follows Parimelazhagar, Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah take the second half as 'even when one is destitute' and the first as 'a greatness not equalled by all the worlds together'. Pope renders it 'Who ne'er consent to beg in utmost need, their worth / Has excellence of greatness that transcends the earth.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தெண்ணீர் அடுபுற்கை ஆயினும் தாள்தந்தது
உண்ணலின் ஊங்கினிய தில்.
transliteration:
Thenneer adupurkai aayinum thaaldhandhadhu
unnalin oonginiya thil.
current_meaning: Even if it is only gruel so thin it looks like clear water, nothing is sweeter than eating what your own effort has earned.
elementary_explanation: A sandwich you made yourself, even a plain one, can taste better than a fancy one someone handed you. The Kural says food you earned with your own work is the sweetest food of all.
university_explanation: Thenneer (தெண்ணீர், 'clear water') describes the gruel: adupurkai (அடுபுற்கை, 'cooked porridge', taken by Puliyur Kesikan as gruel of coarse grass-grain, pullarisi) so watery it looks like clear water. Thaal thandhadhu (தாள்தந்தது, literally 'what the foot/effort gave') is glossed by commentators following Parimelazhagar as what is brought by lawful effort (muyarchi); Puliyur Kesikan adds 'by effort joined with right conduct'. Oonginiyadhu il means 'there is nothing sweeter beyond it'. Pope renders it 'Nothing is sweeter than to taste the toil-won cheer, / Though mess of pottage as tasteless as the water clear.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும் நாவிற்கு
இரவின் இளிவந்த தில்.
transliteration:
Aavirku neerendru irappinum naavirku
iravin ilivandha thil.
current_meaning: Even if you are only begging water for a thirsty cow, nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you need to ask a stranger for water, not even for yourself but for a thirsty animal. The Kural says that even then, asking feels hard and lowering, which shows how heavy begging is.
university_explanation: The couplet chooses the most innocent possible request: aavirku neer (ஆவிற்கு நீர், 'water for a cow'), a deed of dharma, since caring for cattle was held highly meritorious. Puliyur Kesikan, following the Parimelazhagar line, adds that the cow is dying of thirst and the request is made out of compassion; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'asking out of regard for dharma'. Even so, naavirku iravin ilivandhadhu il, 'for the tongue there is nothing more debasing than begging'. The figure is an a fortiori argument: if even this is lowering, begging for oneself is far worse. Pope renders it 'E'en if a draught of water for a cow you ask, / Nought's so distasteful to the tongue as beggar's task.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இரப்பன் இரப்பாரை எல்லாம் இரப்பின்
கரப்பார் இரவன்மின் என்று.
transliteration:
Irappan irappaarai ellaam irappin
karappaar iravanmin endru.
current_meaning: I beg all who beg this one thing: if you must ask, do not ask of those who hide what they have.
elementary_explanation: If you ever really need help, ask someone with a kind and open heart, not someone who pretends to have nothing. The poet even says 'please' to everyone who has to ask for help, because he cares about them.
university_explanation: The couplet is a striking play on one verb, irattal ('to beg'): irappan ('I beg') irappaarai ellaam ('all beggars') irappin ('if you beg') karappaar iravanmin ('do not beg of concealers'). Valluvar thus makes himself a petitioner on behalf of petitioners, a rhetorical humility the commentators note. Karappaar (கரப்பார், 'those who conceal') recalls karappu in ch. 106 and 1061's karavaadhu; the advice, in the line following Parimelazhagar as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar, is that a person forced to ask should at least avoid those who hide what they have. Pope renders it 'One thing I beg of beggars all, 'If beg ye may, / Of those who hide their wealth, beg not, I pray'.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இரவென்னும் ஏமாப்பில் தோணி கரவென்னும்
பார்தாக்கப் பக்கு விடும்.
transliteration:
Iravennum emaappil thoni karavennum
paardhaakkap pakku vidum.
current_meaning: Begging is an unprotected little boat; when it strikes the rock of refusal, it splits apart.
elementary_explanation: Picture a small paper boat floating on a stream. It looks fine until it bumps into a hard rock and breaks. Asking for help is like that boat, and someone's cold 'no' is the rock that breaks it.
university_explanation: The couplet is an extended metaphor (uruvakam): iravu ('begging') is a thoni (தோணி, 'small boat, raft') that is emaappil (ஏமாப்பில், 'without protection, unsafe'), and karavu (கரவு, 'concealment, refusal') is a paar (பார், 'submerged rock, reef'); when it strikes, it pakku vidum ('splits open'). Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line, as in Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah, supply the implied sea: the boat is taken to cross the ocean of poverty. Kalaignar Karunanidhi reads the rock as 'the stone heart that hides what it has and says no'. Pope renders it 'The fragile bark of beggary / Wrecked on denial's rock will lie.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இரவுள்ள உள்ளம் உருகும் கரவுள்ள
உள்ளதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Iravulla ullam urugum karavulla
ulladhooum indrik kedum.
current_meaning: The heart melts at the thought of begging; at the thought of those who hide what they have and refuse, even that melting heart is destroyed.
elementary_explanation: When you see someone who has to ask for help, your heart feels soft and sad. But when you think of someone who has plenty and still says 'I have nothing', your heart feels crushed. The Kural describes both feelings.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two thoughts side by side: iravu ulla (இரவுள்ள, 'when one thinks of begging') the ullam urugum ('heart melts'); karavu ulla ('when one thinks of concealment/refusal') ulladhooum ('even what there is', i.e. the melting heart itself) indrik kedum ('perishes, ceasing to exist'). The pun on ulla ('to think') and ullam ('heart') and ulladhu ('what exists') is characteristic. In the Parimelazhagar line, as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah, the speaker's compassion for beggars is overwhelmed by horror at those who refuse while having plenty. Pope renders it 'The heart will melt away at thought of beggary, / With thought of stern repulse 'twill perish utterly.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கரப்பவர்க்கு யாங்கொளிக்கும் கொல்லோ இரப்பவர்
சொல்லாடப் போஒம் உயிர்.
transliteration:
Karappavarkku yaangolikkum kollo irappavar
sollaadap pooom uyir.
current_meaning: The beggar's life leaves him the moment he hears 'no'; where, then, does the life of the one who says it hide itself?
elementary_explanation: When someone asks for help and hears a cold 'no', it can feel like all their hope has gone. The Kural wonders how the person who said 'no' while having plenty can keep living so easily, as if their heart has gone into hiding.
university_explanation: The chapter ends with a bitter rhetorical question built on a pun: karappavarkku yaangu olikkum kollo ('where does it hide for the concealers?'), the 'it' being uyir ('life'), which in the second line pooom ('goes away', with lengthening for metre) from the irappavar ('askers') as soon as the word of refusal is spoken (sollaada, 'when the word is uttered'). Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line, as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar, read it as amazement: since the refusal kills the asker, the refuser's own life ought to depart too, so where does it hide? Pope renders it 'E'en as he asks, the shamefaced asker dies; / Where shall his spirit hide who help denies?' and paraphrases that the very word that kills the beggar should also kill the refuser. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர் அவரன்ன
ஒப்பாரி யாங்கண்ட தில்.
transliteration:
Makkale polvar kayavar avaranna
oppaari yaangkanda thil.
current_meaning: The base look exactly like human beings; I have never seen a likeness as perfect as theirs between any two other kinds of things.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a shiny plastic apple in a fruit bowl. It looks just like a real apple, but you cannot eat it. Some people are like that: they look like everyone else on the outside, but inside they lack the kindness and goodness that make a real person.
university_explanation: Kayamai (கயமை, 'baseness') closes the Porutpal and its Kudiyiyal section, as a dark mirror to the preceding chapters on nobility of birth, honour, greatness, perfect goodness and courtesy (chs. 96-100). The first couplet is a famous piece of irony: kayavar (கயவர், 'the base') are makkale polvar (மக்களே போல்வர், 'just like humans'), and oppaari (ஒப்பாரி, 'resemblance') so exact is found nowhere else. Parimelazhagar and the commentators who follow him (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan) read it as saying the base share only the outward form of humanity, so that the likeness is complete in shape and absent in substance; Solomon Pappaiah adds that no animal or bird species shows such a perfect double. Pope renders it 'The base resemble men in outward form, I ween; / But counterpart exact to them I've never seen.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நன்றறி வாரிற் கயவர் திருவுடையர்
நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்.
transliteration:
Nandrari vaarir kayavar thiruvudaiyar
nenjaththu avalam ilar.
current_meaning: The base are luckier than those who know what is good, because no worry ever troubles their hearts.
elementary_explanation: Think of two children who broke a vase. One feels bad, says sorry, and worries about it all day. The other just shrugs and goes on playing. The second one looks happier, but only because he does not care about doing right. The Kural is joking: being carefree like that is nothing to envy.
university_explanation: The couplet is sarcastic praise. Nandru arivaar (நன்றறிவார், 'those who know the good') are contrasted with kayavar, who are thiru udaiyar (திருவுடையர், 'possessed of fortune, blessed'), because they have no avalam (அவலம், 'anxiety, grief') in the nenjam (heart). Parimelazhagar explains that the wise are anxious about what is right and its consequences in this world and the next, while the base feel no such care; Puliyur Kesikan glosses nandru as 'what is truly beneficial to oneself'. Kalaignar keeps the irony explicit ('in one way they are fortunate'). Pope: 'Than those of grateful heart the base must luckier be, / Their minds from every anxious thought are free!' Pope's 'grateful' reflects a reading of nandri as 'gratitude'; most Tamil commentators take nandru as 'the good'. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தேவர் அனையர் கயவர் அவருந்தாம்
மேவன செய்தொழுக லான்.
transliteration:
Thevar anaiyar kayavar avarundhaam
mevana seydhozhuga laan.
current_meaning: The base are like the gods, because they too do whatever they please.
elementary_explanation: Gods in stories can do anything they like, and nobody can tell them off. A spoiled bully acts the same way, doing whatever he wants without thinking of anyone else. The Kural jokes that this makes him 'like a god', but it really means he has no self-control at all.
university_explanation: Another ironic comparison: kayavar are thevar anaiyar (தேவர் அனையர், 'like the gods') because they too live mevana seydhu (மேவன செய்து, 'doing what they desire'). Puliyur Kesikan spells out the logic: like the gods, they have no one to restrain them (தம்மை நியமிப்பவர் இல்லாமல்), and Solomon Pappaiah glosses it the same way. Parimelazhagar's reading is that the gods are free because they stand above rules, while the base are 'free' because they ignore them, so the likeness is pure mockery. Kalaignar points to the gods 'of the Puranas' who act on every wish. Pope: 'The base are as the Gods; they too / Do ever what they list to do!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அகப்பட்டி ஆவாரைக் காணின் அவரின்
மிகப்பட்டுச் செம்மாக்கும் கீழ்.
transliteration:
Agappatti aavaaraik kaanin avarin
migappattuch chemmaakkum keezh.
current_meaning: When the base meet people whose conduct is even lower than their own, they swell with pride at being better than them.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a child who got a bad mark on a test. Instead of trying to do better, he finds someone who did even worse and says, 'Ha, at least I'm better than you!' That is what the Kural means: base people feel big by looking down on someone lower.
university_explanation: Keezh (கீழ், 'the low, the base') is the chapter's second word for its subject. The difficult word agappatti (அகப்பட்டி) has divided commentators: Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesikan take aavaar as those who behave even more basely, so that the base man sees them and becomes migappattu (மிகப்பட்டு, 'superior, exalted') and semmaakkum (செம்மாக்கும், 'struts, exults'); Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as 'those who live like dogs, as they please'; Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as 'those beneath them'. The common sense is that baseness takes its self-esteem from someone lower. Pope's 'When base men those behold of conduct vile, / They straight surpass them, and exulting smile' follows the 'conduct vile' reading. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம் எச்சம்
அவாவுண்டேல் உண்டாம் சிறிது.
transliteration:
Achchame keezhgaladhu aasaaram echcham
avaavundel undaam siridhu.
current_meaning: Fear is the main reason the base behave properly; beyond that, they show a little good conduct only when they want something.
elementary_explanation: Some children only behave when the teacher is watching, or when they hope to get a sweet. When nobody is looking and there is no prize, they misbehave. The Kural says base people are like that: they are good only out of fear or for a reward.
university_explanation: Aasaaram (ஆசாரம், from Sanskrit ācāra, 'right conduct, propriety') in the base has two sources only: achcham (அச்சம், 'fear') and, as echcham (எச்சம், 'remainder'), avaa (அவா, 'desire, greed'). Parimelazhagar specifies the fear as fear of the king's punishment, and Puliyur Kesikan follows ('அரசரால் துன்பம் வரும் என்னும் அச்சம்'); Solomon Pappaiah likewise reads it as fear of the government. The second line says that if desire for some gain is present, a little more good conduct appears. The couplet thus defines the base by motive: they have no inner love of virtue. Pope: 'Fear is the base man's virtue; if that fail, / Intense desire some little may avail.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அறைபறை அன்னர் கயவர்தாம் கேட்ட
மறைபிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்க லான்.
transliteration:
Araiparai annar kayavardhaam ketta
maraipirarkku uyththuraikka laan.
current_meaning: The base are like a drum that is beaten to announce news, because they carry every secret they hear straight to others.
elementary_explanation: Long ago, a town crier would beat a big drum and shout the news to the whole village. Some people are like that drum: tell them a secret, and they run off and tell everyone. A good friend keeps a secret safe.
university_explanation: The simile is the araiparai (அறைபறை), the drum beaten in the streets to proclaim royal announcements; Kalaignar names it the thamukku. The base hear a marai (மறை, 'secret, confidential matter') and uyththu uraikkum (உய்த்துரைக்கும், 'carry it to others and tell it'), going out of their way to spread it, as Mu. Varadarasanar stresses (வலிய கொண்டுபோய்). Parimelazhagar's point is that the drum and the base both broadcast what they receive, with no judgement about whether it should be told. Sivayogi Sivakumar adds that the base repeat what they do not themselves understand. Pope: 'The base are like the beaten drum; for, when they hear / The sound the secret out in every neighbour's ear.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார் கயவர் கொடிறுடைக்கும்
கூன்கையர் அல்லா தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Eerngai vidhiraar kayavar kodirudaikkum
koonkaiyar allaa thavarkku.
current_meaning: The base will not even shake the crumbs off their wet hand after eating for anyone except those who would smash their jaw with a clenched fist.
elementary_explanation: After lunch, a few crumbs stick to your hand. Shaking them off for the birds costs you nothing. The Kural says base people will not give even that much to someone gentle who asks, but they will hand over anything to a bully who threatens them.
university_explanation: The image is precise: eerngai (ஈர்ங்கை, 'the wet hand') just washed after a meal, which the base will not even vidhir (விதிர், 'shake') so that a few grains fall to others. They give only to the kodiru udaikkum koonkaiyar (கொடிறுடைக்கும் கூன்கையர், 'those with bent, clenched hands that break the jaw'). Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesikan read koonkai as the fist curled to strike; Kalaignar makes the contrast explicit between the poor, who get nothing, and the thugs, who get what they demand. The couplet joins the chapter's themes of meanness and fear (cf. 1075). Pope: 'From off their moistened hands no clinging grain they shake, / Unless to those with clenched fist their jaws who break.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர் கரும்புபோல்
கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்.
transliteration:
Sollap payanpaduvar saandror karumbupol
kollap payanpadum keezh.
current_meaning: The noble help you as soon as you tell them your need; the base, like sugarcane, give their juice only when they are crushed.
elementary_explanation: To get juice from sugarcane, you have to squeeze and crush it hard. A good person helps you as soon as you ask nicely. A mean person is like the sugarcane: he gives nothing until he is squeezed.
university_explanation: The couplet sets the saandror (சான்றோர், 'the noble, the perfect in virtue', the subject of ch. 99) against the keezh. The noble are solla (சொல்ல, 'on being told') useful: as Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss it, they give as soon as the needy describe their want. The base, karumbu pol (கரும்புபோல், 'like sugarcane'), yield only kolla (கொல்ல, 'on being crushed, killed'). Parimelazhagar takes kolla as being pressed to the point of torment, as cane is crushed in a mill; Pope's prose gloss follows ('only when they are tortured to death'). The image recurs in Tamil didactic poetry, though there the sweetness of crushed cane is sometimes used for the noble who stay sweet under pressure. Pope's verse: 'The good to those will profit yield fair words who use; / The base, like sugar-cane, will profit those who bruise.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின் பிறர்மேல்
வடுக்காண வற்றாகும் கீழ்.
transliteration:
Uduppadhoovum unbadhoovum kaanin pirarmel
vadukkaana vatraagum keezh.
current_meaning: When the base see others wearing good clothes and eating good food, they become experts at finding faults in them.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a classmate gets new shoes and a nice lunch. A jealous child might say, 'Those shoes are ugly' or 'Your lunch smells funny,' just because they feel envious. The Kural says base people do this: they invent faults in others because they cannot stand to see them happy.
university_explanation: The couplet describes envy (azhukkaaru, the subject of ch. 17) turned into fault-finding. Uduppadhum unbadhum (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம், with alapedai lengthening: 'what they wear and what they eat') are the most ordinary signs of others' well-being; on seeing them, the keezh become vatru (வற்று, 'strong, capable') at vadu kaana (வடுக்காண, 'finding a blemish'). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read envy as the cause and deliberate fault-finding as the result; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the base may even try to create a blemish (வடு உண்டாக்கவும் முயல்வான்). Pope: 'If neighbours clothed and fed he see, the base / Is mighty man some hidden fault to trace.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எற்றிற் குரியர் கயவரொன்று உற்றக்கால்
விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து.
transliteration:
Etrir kuriyar kayavarondru utrakkaal
vitrarku uriyar viraindhu.
current_meaning: What are the base good for? When trouble comes, they are quick to sell themselves; that is all they are fit for.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a team captain who, the moment the game gets hard, switches to the other team because they promise him a prize. He cannot be trusted. The Kural says base people are like that: at the first sign of trouble, they will sell out anyone, even themselves.
university_explanation: The chapter, and the whole Porutpal, ends with a rhetorical question: etrirku uriyar (எற்றிற்கு உரியர், 'for what are they fit?'). The answer: ondru utrakkaal (ஒன்று உற்றக்கால், 'when some calamity comes') they are fit vitrarku (விற்றற்கு, 'for selling', i.e. selling themselves) viraindhu (விரைந்து, 'quickly'). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read it as the base hastening to sell themselves to others to escape a misfortune; Puliyur Kesikan adds that they are fit for no other work; Solomon Pappaiah extends it to profit or loss, saying they make themselves others' slaves. The final sarcasm returns to the first couplet: the base have the human form but none of the steadfastness that gives a person worth. Pope: 'For what is base man fit, if griefs assail? / Himself to offer, there and then, for sale!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ கனங்குழை
மாதர்கொல் மாலும்என் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Anangukol aaimayil kollo kananguzhai
maatharkol maalumen nenju.
current_meaning: Is she a goddess, a rare peacock, or a human girl wearing heavy earrings? My heart is bewildered and cannot tell.
elementary_explanation: Imagine seeing a sunset so beautiful that you stop and wonder whether it is real or a painting. The young man in this verse sees a girl for the first time and is so amazed that he cannot decide whether she is a goddess, a lovely peacock, or an ordinary girl.
university_explanation: This kural opens the Kamattuppal and its Kalaviyal (the section on premarital, 'secret' love), voicing the hero's (talaivan's) first sight of the heroine. The chapter title combines takai (தகை, 'beauty, grace'), anangu (அணங்கு, a goddess or spirit that afflicts those who approach it) and uruttal (உறுத்தல், 'causing'), so it means the distress her beauty inflicts. The three-way doubt, anangu-kol, aaimayil-kollo, maathar-kol (goddess? choice peahen? woman?), is a classical Tamil figure of bewilderment (aiyam), and maalum (மாலும், 'is confused, infatuated') names the state. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses kananguzhai as 'a woman wearing heavy ear-ornaments', the detail that hints she is human after all; Pope renders 'Goddess? or peafowl rare?... All wildered is my mind!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
நோக்கினாள் நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல் தாக்கணங்கு
தானைக்கொண் டன்ன துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Nokkinaal nokkethir nokkuthal thaakkanangu
thaanaikkon tanna thudaiththu.
current_meaning: When she returns my look, her answering glance is like an attacking goddess who has brought a whole army with her.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever been looked at so seriously that you suddenly felt shy and could not look back? Here the young man looks at the girl, and when she looks back at him he feels as if an entire army has charged at him.
university_explanation: The kural turns on the repeated root nokku (நோக்கு, 'look'): nokkinaal ('she who looked'), nokkethir ('against my look') and nokkuthal ('the looking back'). Thaakkanangu (தாக்கணங்கு) is an anangu that strikes or attacks on its own, and thaanai (தானை) is an army; Mu. Varadarasanar explains that her return glance is like such a self-attacking deity arriving with a whole army. Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line take the point to be that one glance already wounds, so a returned glance doubles the assault. Pope renders: 'As if the matchless goddess' hand / Led forth an armed band.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
பண்டறியேன் கூற்றென் பதனை இனியறிந்தேன்
பெண்டகையால் பேரமர்க் கட்டு.
transliteration:
Pandariyen kootren pathanai iniyarinthen
pendakaiyaal peramark kattu.
current_meaning: I never knew before what they call Death; now I know it: it has a woman's grace and large eyes that make war.
elementary_explanation: People sometimes say a scary film 'nearly killed' them, even though they were safe. The young man jokes in the same way: he had only heard of Death in stories, but now he has met it, in the shape of a girl with big, powerful eyes.
university_explanation: Kootru (கூற்று) is Death personified, Yama, the 'one who divides' body from life. Pandariyen ('I did not know before') and iniyarinthen ('now I have learned') frame a mock discovery. The second line packs pen-takai (பெண்டகை, 'womanly grace') with per-amar-kan (பேரமர்க்கண், 'large eyes that do battle'); Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as 'it has a woman's nature and large eyes that make war', while Kalaignar speaks of eye-arrows. The commentarial tradition treats the hyperbole as the lover's helplessness, not a moral judgment on the woman. Pope: 'Death's form I formerly / Knew not; but now 'tis plain to me; / He comes in lovely maiden's guise.' Identical on both web sources.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றத்தால் பெண்டகைப்
பேதைக்கு அமர்த்தன கண்.
transliteration:
Kandaar uyirunnum thottraththaal pendakaip
pethaikku amarththana kan.
current_meaning: This gentle, innocent girl has eyes that seem to drink the life of anyone who sees them, so her eyes are at odds with her soft nature.
elementary_explanation: Think of a kitten with huge, shining eyes: it is small and gentle, yet one look can make everyone in the room stop what they are doing. The young man sees that the girl is shy and gentle, but her eyes are so powerful that they seem to belong to someone much fiercer.
university_explanation: Uyir-unnum (உயிருண்ணும்) means 'devouring life', and kandaar (கண்டார்) 'those who see', so her eyes have a look that eats the life of every viewer. Pethai (பேதை) here means an innocent young girl, not a 'fool', and pen-takai (பெண்டகை) is womanly grace. The key verb amarththana (அமர்த்தன) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as 'were at variance with one another', i.e. the eyes contradict her gentle nature; Solomon Pappaiah adds that they 'war against' her character and understanding. Pope renders: 'In sweet simplicity, / A woman's gracious form hath she; / But yet those eyes, that drink my life, / Are with the form at strife!' Identical on both sources.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ மடவரல்
நோக்கமிம் மூன்றும் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Kootramo kanno pinaiyo madavaral
nokkamim moondrum udaiththu.
current_meaning: Is it Death, is it an eye, or is it a shy doe? This young girl's look has all three natures at once.
elementary_explanation: Some things can be several things at once: a rainbow is pretty, a bit mysterious and gone in a moment. The young man finds the girl's look like that. It is powerful enough to knock him over, warm like a friendly eye, and shy like a little deer.
university_explanation: The question again uses the doubting particle -o: kootramo (கூற்றமோ, 'Death?'), kanno (கண்ணோ, 'an eye?'), pinaiyo (பிணையோ, 'a hind/doe?'). Madavaral (மடவரல்) is a young, innocent woman, and nokkam (நோக்கம்) her look. Commentators explain the three qualities differently: Mu. Varadarasanar simply lists Death, eye and doe; Solomon Pappaiah reads the eye as a glance that spreads all over the viewer's body and the doe as a timid, fearful look; Puliyur Kesikan has 'the afflicting Death, the darting eye, the startled doe'. The point is that one look combines danger, warmth and shyness. Pope: 'Is it death's dart? or eye's bright beams? / Or fawn's shy glance? All three appear.' Identical on both sources.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
கொடும்புருவம் கோடா மறைப்பின் நடுங்கஞர்
செய்யல மன்இவள் கண்.
transliteration:
Kodumpuruvam kodaa maraippin nadungagnar
seyyala manival kan.
current_meaning: If her curved eyebrows would only stay straight and screen her eyes, her eyes would not cause me this trembling distress.
elementary_explanation: When the sun is too bright, a cap with a peak shades your eyes so you are not dazzled. The young man wishes her eyebrows would act like that cap and shade her eyes, so her look would not make him so nervous.
university_explanation: Kodum-puruvam (கொடும்புருவம்) means the 'curved' or 'cruel' brows; kodum carries both senses, so the curve itself is accused. Kodaa (கோடா, 'without bending') and maraippin (மறைப்பின், 'if they hid') give the wish: if the brows stayed straight and screened the eyes. Nadung-agnar (நடுங்கஞர்) is 'trembling distress', and man (மன்) adds regret, 'surely they would not...'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both read it as 'if the bent brows stood straight and hid them, her eyes would not cause me trembling sorrow'. The image draws on the Indian convention of brows as a drawn bow from which the eyes shoot. Pope: 'If cruel eye-brow's bow, / Unbent, would veil those glances now.' Identical on both sources.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம் மாதர்
படாஅ முலைமேல் துகில்.
transliteration:
Kadaaak kalitrinmer katpadaam maathar
padaaa mulaimel thukil.
current_meaning: The garment draped over the maiden's bosom is like the cloth placed over the eyes of a raging elephant: a covering that keeps a dangerous power in check.
elementary_explanation: At festivals, big temple elephants sometimes wear a decorated cloth over their faces. It looks beautiful, but it also helps keep the elephant calm. The young man thinks the scarf the girl wears works the same way, both lovely and protective.
university_explanation: Kadaaak kalitru (கடாஅக் களிறு) is a bull elephant in must (mada), and katpadaam (கட்படாம்) the cloth hung over its face and eyes to keep it from charging. Thukil (துகில்) is fine cloth worn by the maathar (மாதர், young woman). The lengthened forms kadaaa and padaaa are alapedai, vowel extension for metre. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read the comparison as protective: the covering stops her beauty from 'killing' the onlooker, just as the face-cloth restrains the elephant. Pope: 'As veil o'er angry eyes / Of raging elephant that lies, / The silken cincture's folds invest / This maiden's panting breast.' Identical on both sources.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
ஒண்ணுதற் கோஒ உடைந்ததே ஞாட்பினுள்
நண்ணாரும் உட்குமென் பீடு.
transliteration:
Onnuthar koo udainthathe gnaatpinul
nannaarum utkumen peedu.
current_meaning: Alas! My might, which made even my enemies tremble on the battlefield, has broken before her bright forehead alone.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a champion wrestler who has never lost, but who becomes shy and tongue-tied when he meets someone he really admires. The young man is a brave warrior, yet one look at the girl's shining face makes all his toughness melt away.
university_explanation: On-nuthal (ஒண்ணுதல்) is a 'bright forehead', a standard metonymy for the heroine. Koo (கோஒ) is an exclamation of dismay lengthened by alapedai. Gnaatpu (ஞாட்பு) is the battlefield, nannaar (நண்ணார்) foes (literally 'those who do not draw near', i.e. are not friends), utkum (உட்கும்) 'fear', and peedu (பீடு) 'valour, prowess'. Mu. Varadarasanar reads: 'my strength, which made even foes fear in battle, has been defeated by her bright forehead'; Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah take nannaar as including those who only heard of his fame. The hero (talaivan) of Tamil akam poetry is ideally a warrior, so the defeat is sharpened. Pope: 'my might, / That awed my foemen in the fight, / By lustre of that beaming brow / Borne down, lies broken now!' Identical on both sources.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
பிணையேர் மடநோக்கும் நாணும் உடையாட்கு
அணியெவனோ ஏதில தந்து.
transliteration:
Pinaiyer madanokkum naanum udaiyaatku
aniyevano ethila thanthu.
current_meaning: She already has the gentle, doe-like look and natural modesty; what use are other ornaments, which have nothing to do with her, on such a girl?
elementary_explanation: A flower in a garden is already beautiful; you do not need to paint it or stick glitter on it. The young man feels the same about the girl: her kind eyes and shyness are her real jewels, so ordinary jewellery adds nothing.
university_explanation: Pinai-er (பிணையேர்) means 'like a doe', mada-nokku (மடநோக்கு) 'an innocent, gentle look', and naanum (நாணும்) 'and modesty'. Naanam (நாணம்) is one of the classical feminine virtues in Tamil poetics, alongside madam (innocence), accham (fear) and payirppu (delicacy). Ethila (ஏதில) is 'alien, unrelated', so other ornaments are foreign to her true beauty. Mu. Varadarasanar asks why one should put unrelated jewels on her; Kalaignar contrasts natural (iyarkai) and artificial (seyarkai) ornaments. Pope: 'Like tender fawn's her eye; / Clothed on is she with modesty; / What added beauty can be lent / By alien ornament?' Identical on both sources.

chapter_title: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty
tamil:
உண்டார்கண் அல்லது அடுநறாக் காமம்போல்
கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று.
transliteration:
Undaarkan allathu adunaraak kaamampol
kandaar makizhseydhal indru.
current_meaning: Strong drink delights only those who drink it; it cannot, as love does, delight people who merely look.
elementary_explanation: A treat only makes you happy once you eat it. But seeing someone you love, like a parent coming home, makes you happy just by looking. The young man says love is special in this way: just seeing her fills him with joy.
university_explanation: Undaar (உண்டார்) is 'those who have drunk' and kandaar (கண்டார்) 'those who have seen'; the pairing undaar / kandaar carries the whole comparison. Adu-nara (அடுநறா) is literally 'cooked (boiled, distilled) toddy', i.e. strong drink, and makizh-seythal (மகிழ்செய்தல்) is 'causing delight or intoxication'. Mu. Varadarasanar: toddy intoxicates only those who drink it, not, like kaamam, those who merely see it. The verse closes the chapter by turning the hero's distress into joy, and its praise of love over drink sits easily with the Kural's earlier chapter against intoxicants (Kallunnaamai, ch. 93). Pope: 'The palm-tree's fragrant wine, / To those who taste yields joys divine; / But love hath rare felicity / For those that only see!' Identical on both sources.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
இருநோக்கு இவளுண்கண் உள்ளது ஒருநோக்கு
நோய்நோக்கொன் றந்நோய் மருந்து.
transliteration:
Irunokku ivalunkan ulladhu orunokku
noinokkon randhnoi marundhu.
current_meaning: Her darkened eyes hold two kinds of look: one look gives me the ache of love, and the other is the very medicine for that ache.
elementary_explanation: Think of a new classmate who is very shy. When she looks at you, you feel all fluttery and nervous inside. But when she looks again and gives a small friendly smile, the nervous feeling goes away. The same eyes made the worry and then made it better.
university_explanation: Chapter 110 opens the second stage of the kalaviyal (the section on secret, premarital love): after the first sight of ch. 109 (Takaiyananguruttal), the hero now reads the heroine’s kurippu (குறிப்பு, ‘sign, inward intention’) for proof that his love is returned. The chapter shares its title with ch. 71 of Porutpal, where kurippu arithal means reading a king’s mind, so the same art of reading the face is moved from the court to love. Unkan (உண்கண்) means eyes that have ‘eaten’ collyrium (mai), that is, kohl-darkened eyes, and every gloss on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) reads the two looks as a nōy nōkku (நோய் நோக்கு, the look that causes love-sickness) and a remedy-look; in the line of Parimelazhagar the second look is her answering sign of consent, which ends his uncertainty. Pope renders: ‘A double witchery have glances of her liquid eye; / One glance is glance that brings me pain; the other heals again.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம் காமத்தில்
செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது.
transliteration:
Kankalavu kollum sirunokkam kaamaththil
sempaakam andru peridhu.
current_meaning: The quick glance she steals at me when I am not looking is not merely half of love’s joy; it is more than half.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever caught a friend secretly peeking at the drawing you were making, and then looking away? That tiny peek tells you they really like it, maybe even more than if they had said so out loud. A small secret look can say a lot.
university_explanation: Kan kalavu kollum (கண் களவு கொள்ளும்) is literally ‘the eye that steals’: a look taken by stealth (kalavu, the same word that names the whole kalavu, or secret-love, phase). Ciru nōkkam (சிறுநோக்கம்) is the brief, narrowed glance, which Puliyur Kesikan glosses as arukiya nōkkam, a sparing look cast without his knowledge. Sempākam (செம்பாகம்) means ‘exact half’; the commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar: nērpāti anru, atai vida periya pakuti) agree the stolen glance is greater than half of kāmam, the joy of union, because it reveals that his love is returned. Pope: ‘The furtive glance, that gleams one instant bright, / Is more than half of love’s supreme delight.’ No textual variants appear on the two source sites.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
நோக்கினாள் நோக்கி இறைஞ்சினாள் அஃதவள்
யாப்பினுள் அட்டிய நீர்.
transliteration:
Nokkinaal nokki irainjinaal aqdhaval
yaappinul attiya neer.
current_meaning: She looked at me, and having looked, she bowed her head; that gesture was water poured on the growing plant of our love.
elementary_explanation: Imagine planting a seed with a friend. Every time you water it, it grows a little. When someone shyly looks at you and then looks down with a little smile, it is like giving water to the seed of a new friendship.
university_explanation: Iraiñcināḷ (இறைஞ்சினாள்) means ‘she bowed, lowered her head’, the classic sign of nāṇam (நாணம், maidenly modesty) that the hero reads as consent. The key image is yāppu (யாப்பு), which the commentators take as the bond or bed of love: Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the love she is nurturing, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the ‘crop’ (payir) of love, and Puliyur Kesikan as the anpup-payir watered by her sign. Aṭṭiya nīr (அட்டிய நீர்) is water poured into a channel or plot, an agricultural metaphor in keeping with the marutam landscape of settled love. Pope: ‘She looked, and looking drooped her head: / On springing shoot of love ’tis water shed!’ The text is the same on both source sites.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
யான்நோக்கும் காலை நிலன்நோக்கும் நோக்காக்கால்
தான்நோக்கி மெல்ல நகும்.
transliteration:
Yaannokkum kaalai nilannokkum nokkaakkaal
thaannokki mella nagum.
current_meaning: When I look at her, she looks at the ground; when I do not look, she looks at me and smiles softly to herself.
elementary_explanation: Picture a shy kid in class. Whenever you turn to look, they quickly stare at their desk. But when you turn back to your book, you can feel them peeking at you with a small smile. That little game means they want to be your friend.
university_explanation: The couplet builds on a chiastic play of nōkku (நோக்கு, ‘look’): yān nōkkum kālai (when I look) she looks at nilan (நிலன், the ground); nōkkākkāl (when I do not look) she looks and mella nakum (மெல்ல நகும், smiles gently). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take nakum as smiling or rejoicing to herself, and Kalaignar adds that this is a sign announcing her love. Commentators in the Parimelazhagar tradition treat the lowered gaze as nāṇam and the secret smile as the kurippu of consent. Pope: ‘I look on her: her eyes are on the ground the while: / I look away: she looks on me with timid smile.’ The two source sites agree on the text.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
குறிக்கொண்டு நோக்காமை அல்லால் ஒருகண்
சிறக்கணித்தாள் போல நகும்.
transliteration:
Kurikkondu nokkaamai allaal orukan
sirakkaniththaal poala nagum.
current_meaning: She does not look straight at me; yet, as if narrowing one eye in a sidelong look, she smiles to herself.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes a friend pretends not to watch you, but you catch them looking out of the corner of their eye with a little grin. They are not really ignoring you; they are just being shy and playful.
university_explanation: Kuṟikkoṇṭu nōkkāmai (குறிக்கொண்டு நோக்காமை) is ‘not looking with a fixed aim’, that is, avoiding a direct gaze. The difficult word ciṟakkaṇittāḷ (சிறக்கணித்தாள்) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as ‘narrowing one eye’ (oru kaṇṇaic curukki), while Puliyur Kesikan takes it as tilting one eye to one side; Pope’s ‘smiling side-long glance’ follows the second sense, and the explanatory gloss on ytamizh renders it as looking ‘with a half-closed eye’. Either way the commentators read the sidelong smile as a kurippu that she returns his love while seeming not to. The Tamil is the same on both source sites.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
உறாஅ தவர்போல் சொலினும் செறாஅர்சொல்
ஒல்லை உணரப் படும்.
transliteration:
Uraaa thavarpol solinum seraaarsol
ollai unarap padum.
current_meaning: Even when those who bear no anger speak as though they were strangers, the true meaning of their words is quickly understood.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes a friend says, ‘I don’t care, go away!’ but they are smiling and not really cross. You can tell right away they are only pretending. Kind people cannot hide their kindness for long.
university_explanation: Uṟāatavar (உறாஅதவர்) and ceṟāar (செறாஅர்) both carry the long-vowel extension (alapeṭai) used for metre: ‘those who are not intimate’ and ‘those who are not angry’. Ollai (ஒல்லை) means ‘quickly’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses: though they speak outwardly like strangers without affection, the words of those with no enmity within are soon recognised; Solomon Pappaiah sets the scene with her reply ‘who are you?’ to his approach, and Kalaignar says the love she hides behind harsh words soon shows through. Puliyur Kesikan reads that the result (payan) of such words is soon felt. Pope: ‘Though with their lips affection they disown, / Yet, when they hate us not, ’tis quickly known.’ No variants on the two source sites.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
செறாஅச் சிறுசொல்லும் செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும்
உறாஅர்போன்று உற்றார் குறிப்பு.
transliteration:
Seraaach chirusollum setraarpol nokkum
uraaarpondru utraar kurippu.
current_meaning: Small sharp words that carry no anger, and looks that seem hostile, are the signs of those who love while acting like strangers.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever seen two best friends tease each other, saying ‘You’re so annoying!’ while grinning? Their pretend-grumpy faces are really a sign of how close they are. Sometimes people who like each other act as if they don’t.
university_explanation: The couplet balances ceṟāac ciṟucol (செறாஅச் சிறுசொல், ‘little words that are not angry’) against ceṟṟār pōl nōkku (செற்றார்போல் நோக்கு, ‘a look like that of enemies’), and names both the kuṟippu of uṟṟār (உற்றார், intimates, lovers) who behave uṟāar pōnṟu (like those not intimate). Mu. Varadarasanar reads ciṟucol as kaṭuñcol, harsh words that hold no hostility; Kalaignar speaks of lovers ‘acting’ like strangers outwardly while loving within; Solomon Pappaiah frames it as the hero now understanding her earlier coldness. The couplet completes the thought of 1096 by naming the signs. Pope: ‘The slighting words that anger feign, while eyes their love reveal, / Are signs of those that love, but would their love conceal.’ Text identical on both sites.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
அசையியற்கு உண்டாண்டோர் ஏஎர்யான் நோக்கப்
பசையினள் பைய நகும்.
transliteration:
Asaiyiyarku undaandor eeryaan nokkap
pasaiyinal paiya nagum.
current_meaning: When I look at her imploringly, she softens and smiles gently; in that moment this delicate girl has a special grace.
elementary_explanation: When you look at someone with a hopeful, friendly face, and their serious look melts into a soft smile, it feels wonderful. That smile is a sign they are happy to be your friend.
university_explanation: Asaiyiyal (அசையியல்) is ‘she whose nature sways’, a soft, delicate girl; ēer (ஏஎர், ēr with alapeṭai) means beauty or grace, and āṇṭu (ஆண்டு) ‘then, there’. Pasaiyinaḷ (பசையினள்) is ‘she who has softened, become tender’. The commentators differ on ēer: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as a new beauty she has at that moment; Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan read the line as saying there is a sign (kuṟippu) or token of goodness in her smile; Kesikan also understands yān nōkka as ‘when I looked as if begging’. The ytamizh Sivayogi gloss reads differently again, showing real interpretive variety in this couplet. Pope: ‘I gaze, the tender maid relents the while; / And, oh the matchless grace of that soft smile!’ Text identical on both source sites.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
ஏதிலார் போலப் பொதுநோக்கு நோக்குதல்
காதலார் கண்ணே உள.
transliteration:
Edhilaar polap podhunokku nokkudhal
kaadhalaar kanne ula.
current_meaning: To look at each other with a plain, ordinary look, as if they were strangers, is a habit found only among those who are in love.
elementary_explanation: Two good friends might act normal in front of everyone, as if they hardly know each other, but they still understand each other perfectly. Only close friends can play that ‘we’re just strangers’ game.
university_explanation: Ētilār (ஏதிலார்) means ‘strangers, people with no connection’, and potu nōkku (பொதுநோக்கு) is a ‘common’ or neutral look, the kind one gives anyone in a crowd. Kātalār kaṇṇē uḷa (காதலார் கண்ணே உள) asserts, with the emphatic -ē, that this is found only among lovers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as lovers outwardly looking like strangers while loving within; Kalaignar specifies that they do this in public places; Puliyur Kesikan applies it to both lovers looking at each other. The couplet draws a general rule from the hero’s experience in 1096-1098. Pope: ‘The look indifferent, that would its love disguise, / Is only read aright by lovers’ eyes.’ Text identical on both source sites.

chapter_title: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)
tamil:
கண்ணொடு கண்இணை நோக்கொக்கின் வாய்ச்சொற்கள்
என்ன பயனும் இல.
transliteration:
Kannodu kaninai nokkokkin vaaichchorkal
enna payanum ila.
current_meaning: When eye meets eye and the looks agree, the words of the mouth are of no use at all.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes you and your best friend just look at each other and both burst out laughing, because you are thinking the same thing. You didn’t need to say a single word. Your eyes did all the talking.
university_explanation: Kaṇṇoṭu kaṇ iṇai nōkku okkin (கண்ணொடு கண்இணை நோக்கொக்கின்): ‘if the pair of eyes agree in look with the other pair’. Okkin (‘if they match’) is the key word: mutual, matching love, not one-sided longing. Vāyccoṟkaḷ (வாய்ச்சொற்கள்) are words of the mouth, which then have enna payanum ila, ‘no use whatever’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss: when eyes join in equal love, spoken words become unnecessary; Puliyur Kesikan specifies the two who are united in kāmam. The couplet closes the chapter by stating its principle: in love, the eyes are the true language, which is why the whole chapter has been about reading looks. Pope: ‘When eye to answering eye reveals the tale of love, / All words that lips can say must useless prove.’ The ytamizh transliteration writes kaN-inai, matching the Tamil கண்இணை; the text is identical on both sites.

tamil:
கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்
ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள.
transliteration:
Kandukettu unduyirththu utrariyum aimpulanum
ondhodi kanne ula.
current_meaning: All the joys that the five senses know, by seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching, are found together in this one woman with bright bangles.
elementary_explanation: Think of the best day of a holiday: you see the lights, hear the music, taste the sweets, smell the flowers and feel a warm hug. Usually each good thing comes from a different place. The lover in this verse says that, for him, every one of those good feelings comes from one single person he loves.
university_explanation: Chapter 111 belongs to the kalaviyal (the section on premarital, secret love) and follows the exchange of glances in ch. 110; in the commentary tradition that runs through Parimelazhagar it voices the hero’s (talaivan’s) joy after the lovers’ first union, and nearly every couplet is his speech. The five verbs kaṇṭu (seeing), kēṭṭu (hearing), uṇṭu (eating, tasting), uyirttu (breathing in, smelling) and uṟṟu (touching) name the aimpulaṉ (ஐம்புலன், the five senses or sense-pleasures) in their classical order, and kaṇṇē uḷa means ‘are located in her’ (kaṇ as a locative). Oṇtoṭi (ஒண்தொடி, ‘she of the bright bangle’) is a standard metonymy for a young woman; the commentators on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesikan) gloss the line as all five sense-joys being present in her alone. Pope renders: ‘All joys that senses five- sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch- can give, / In this resplendent armlets-bearing damsel live!’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the sung version printed on thirukkural.net writes ஒண்டொடி, an ordinary sandhi spelling of the same word.

tamil:
பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிறமன் அணியிழை
தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து.
transliteration:
Pinikku marundhu piraman aniyizhai
thannoikkuth thaane marundhu.
current_meaning: For other illnesses the medicine is something different from the illness; but for the love-sickness this jewelled girl causes, she herself is the only medicine.
elementary_explanation: When you miss your best friend who has moved away, no toy or sweet makes the sad feeling go. The only thing that fixes it is seeing that friend again. The person you miss is both the reason you feel sad and the cure.
university_explanation: The couplet sets ordinary medicine against love: for a piṇi (பிணி, disease) the marundu (மருந்து, remedy) is piṟa (‘something other’), while the nōy (நோய், sickness) caused by the aṇiyiḻai (அணியிழை, ‘she of fine jewels’) is cured only by her. Man in piṟaman is an expletive particle (asai) with no meaning of its own, as the commentators note. Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the logic: remedies usually have a nature opposite to the disease, yet here the cause and the cure are the same. The idea continues ch. 110’s opening kural (1091), where one glance wounds and another heals, and moves it from the look to union itself. Pope: ‘Disease and medicine antagonists we surely see; / This maid, to pain she gives, herself is remedy.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள் துயிலின் இனிதுகொல்
தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு.
transliteration:
Thaamveezhvaar mendrol thuyilin inidhukol
thaamaraik kannaan ulagu.
current_meaning: Can the heaven of the lotus-eyed god be any sweeter than sleep resting on the soft shoulder of the one you love?
elementary_explanation: Imagine falling asleep safe and warm after a long trip, with someone who loves you right beside you. Grown-ups sometimes say heaven is the happiest place there is. This verse asks, with a smile, whether even heaven could feel better than that peaceful, loved feeling.
university_explanation: The couplet is a rhetorical question: is tāmaraik kaṇṇāṉ ulagu (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு), ‘the world of the lotus-eyed one’, sweeter than sleep on the soft shoulders (meṉṟōḷ) of those one loves (tām vīḻvār)? Commentators in Parimelazhagar’s line identify the lotus-eyed one with Tirumal (Vishnu) and his world with his heaven (Vaikuntha), and Solomon Pappaiah glosses it this way; Kalaignar frames it as a sceptical question about what people call ‘the lotus-eyed one’s world’. The particle kol (கொல்) marks doubt, so the answer implied is ‘no’. The verse is one of the few places where the Kural names a deity by an epithet, and it ranks the joy of love above the reward of heaven only playfully, inside the love-poetry convention. Pope: ‘Than rest in her soft arms to whom the soul is giv’n, / Is any sweeter joy in his, the Lotus-eyed-one’s heaven?’ Text identical on both source sites.

tamil:
நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும்
தீயாண்டுப் பெற்றாள் இவள்.
transliteration:
Neengin theruum kurugungaal thannennum
theeyaandup petraal ival.
current_meaning: If I move away it burns me, and if I come near it cools me; where did she find such a strange fire?
elementary_explanation: Have you ever felt grumpy and hot inside when you had to leave someone you love, and calm again as soon as you were back together? The lover says she must own a magic fire: it burns when you go away and feels cool and gentle when you come close. Real fire does the opposite!
university_explanation: The conceit rests on reversing the nature of fire: ordinary fire burns those who come near and leaves those who move away, but this fire teṟūum (தெறூஉம், ‘burns’, with the vowel lengthening called uyiraḷapeṭai for metre) when he leaves (nīṅkiṉ) and taṇ eṉṉum (‘turns cool’) when he draws near (kuṟukuṅkāl). The question tī yāṇṭup peṟṟāḷ (‘from where did she get the fire?’) is wonder rather than inquiry, and every gloss on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Kalaignar) calls it a putumaiyāṉa tī, a ‘new, unheard-of fire’; Solomon Pappaiah adds that she has lit it in his heart. The couplet anticipates the separation chapters of the kaṟpiyal, where absence is described as burning. Pope: ‘Withdraw, it burns; approach, it soothes the pain; / Whence did the maid this wondrous fire obtain?’ Text identical on both source sites.

tamil:
வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே
தோட்டார் கதுப்பினாள் தோள்.
transliteration:
Vetta pozhudhin avaiyavai polume
thottaar kadhuppinaal thol.
current_meaning: The embrace of the girl whose hair is full of flowers gives joy just as each longed-for thing does at the very moment it is wanted.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a magic lunchbox that always holds exactly what you are hungry for: soup when you are cold, ice cream when you are hot. The lover says that being close to the one he loves is like that box: it always gives the right happiness at the right time.
university_explanation: Vēṭṭa poḻutiṉ avaiyavai pōlumē says that her shoulders (tōḷ, standing for her embrace) are ‘like each of those things at the time they are desired’: the comparison is with any object of desire enjoyed exactly when wished for. Tōṭṭār katuppiṉāḷ (தோட்டார் கதுப்பினாள்) is ‘she whose tresses (katuppu) are full of petals or flowers (tōṭu)’, an epithet of the adorned beloved. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read it as ‘whenever one unites with her, she gives the delight of whatever one desires’, and Kalaignar compares it to a wished-for thing arriving whenever wished; the image recalls the wish-granting tree and cow of Indian lore, though the Kural does not name them. Pope: ‘In her embrace, whose locks with flowery wreaths are bound, / Each varied form of joy the soul can wish is found.’ Text identical on both source sites.

tamil:
உறுதோறு உயிர்தளிர்ப்பத் தீண்டலால் பேதைக்கு
அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்.
transliteration:
Urudhoru uyirthalirppath theendalaal pedhaikku
amizhdhin iyandrana thol.
current_meaning: Every time I hold her, her touch makes my wilting life put out fresh shoots; this innocent girl’s shoulders must be made of nectar.
elementary_explanation: Think of a droopy plant that perks up the moment you give it water. When someone you love gives you a hug after a hard day, you can feel the same way. The lover says her hugs work like magic drink that makes him feel alive and fresh again every single time.
university_explanation: Uyir taḷirppa (உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப, ‘so that life puts forth tender shoots’) is a plant image: the lover’s withered life sprouts again, as Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah gloss it (vāṭiya uyir taḷirkka, ‘the wilted life sprouting’). Uṟutōṟu means ‘every time I come close’, and from this repeated reviving effect the lover infers that her shoulders are amiḻtiṉ iyaṉṟaṉa (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன), ‘fashioned of amizhtu’, the nectar of immortality (Sanskrit amṛta). Pētai (பேதை) here means a simple, innocent young woman; it is also the name of the youngest of the seven traditional stages of womanhood, but the commentators read it in the general sense. Pope: ‘Ambrosia are the simple maiden’s arms; when I attain / Their touch, my withered life puts forth its buds again!’ Text identical on both source sites.

tamil:
தம்மில் இருந்து தமதுபாத்து உண்டற்றால்
அம்மா அரிவை முயக்கு.
transliteration:
Thammil irundhu thamadhupaaththu undatraal
ammaa arivai muyakku.
current_meaning: The embrace of this lovely, fair-skinned young woman is like living in one’s own home and eating what one has earned, after sharing it with others.
elementary_explanation: Remember how good it feels to eat a meal you helped cook, at your own table, after giving some to your friends? It feels honest and happy and safe. The lover says being close to the one he loves gives that same warm, at-home happiness.
university_explanation: The simile draws on the householder ideal of the Arattuppal: tammil iruntu (‘dwelling in one’s own home’), tamatu (‘one’s own’, i.e. what one has earned) pāttu uṇṭaṟṟāl (‘like eating after dividing and sharing it’). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses pāttu as distributing one’s earnings to others before eating, Solomon Pappaiah as sharing with one’s own people, and Puliyur Kesikan more narrowly as eating one’s own portion; all agree that the pleasure is one of independence, rightful ownership and generosity. Ammā is read as am (‘beautiful’) plus māmai (‘the dark-gold complexion praised in Tamil poetry’), and arivai (அரிவை) is a young woman, also the name of one of the seven traditional stages of womanhood. Muyakku (முயக்கு) is ‘embrace’. Pope: ‘As when one eats from household store, with kindly grace / Sharing his meal: such is this golden maid’s embrace.’ Text identical on both source sites.

tamil:
வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே வளியிடை
போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு.
transliteration:
Veezhum iruvarkku inidhe valiyidai
pozhap padaaa muyakku.
current_meaning: Sweet to two people who love each other is an embrace so close that not even a breath of wind can pass between them.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever hugged someone so tightly that you felt like one person? The verse says that for two people who love each other, the sweetest hug is one so close that not even a tiny puff of air could slip in between.
university_explanation: Vīḻum iruvar (வீழும் இருவர், ‘two who desire each other’) stresses that the love is mutual, and the embrace (muyakku) is one that vaḷi iṭai pōḻap paṭāa (‘is not split apart in the middle by the wind’). Paṭāa carries the metrical lengthening (aḷapeṭai) also seen in teṟūum of kural 1104. Every gloss on both sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) reads it as an embrace so close that even air cannot enter. Pope, characteristically, turns the image moral: ‘Sweet is the strict embrace of those whom fond affection binds, / Where no dissevering breath of discord entrance finds’, treating the wind as discord, a reading the Tamil commentators do not share. Text identical on both source sites.

tamil:
ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல் இவைகாமம்
கூடியார் பெற்ற பயன்.
transliteration:
Oodal unardhal punardhal ivaikaamam
koodiyaar petra payan.
current_meaning: A lovers’ quarrel, making it up, and coming together again: these are the rewards that those whose love has been fulfilled enjoy.
elementary_explanation: Best friends sometimes have a small grumpy fight, then say sorry, and then feel even closer than before. The verse says that this little circle of a pretend sulk, making up and being together again is one of the sweet parts of love.
university_explanation: The couplet names the three-part movement that structures the closing chapters of the Kamattuppal: ūṭal (ஊடல், the lover’s feigned or playful sulking), uṇartal (உணர்தல், its resolution, the partner understanding and appeasing it) and puṇartal (புணர்தல், reunion). Kāmam kūṭiyār (‘those in whom love has come together’, i.e. lovers whose love is fulfilled) obtain these as payaṉ, ‘fruit’. Solomon Pappaiah places it explicitly in married life (a small tiff, reconciliation, then reunion), Puliyur Kesikan adds that the sulk should be kept within measure (aḷavōṭu), and Kalaignar gives a slightly different reading of uṇartal. The triad anticipates chapters 131-133 (Pulavi, Pulavi Nuṇukkam, Ūṭaluvakai), where the delight of the lovers’ quarrel becomes the main theme. Pope: ‘The jealous variance, the healing of the strife, reunion gained: / These are the fruits from wedded love obtained.’ Text identical on both source sites.

tamil:
அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்றால் காமம்
செறிதோறும் சேயிழை மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Aridhoru ariyaamai kandatraal kaamam
seridhorum seyizhai maattu.
