current_meaning: The more one learns, the more one discovers how much one does not yet know; so too, each time I come close to my jewelled beloved, my love finds something new.
elementary_explanation: When you read one good book about space, you find out there are a hundred more things about space you never knew. The more you learn, the more there is to learn! The lover says love is like that: the more time he spends with the one he loves, the more new things he finds to love.
university_explanation: The chapter ends with a celebrated simile from learning: aṟitōṟu aṟiyāmai kaṇṭaṟṟāl (‘like discovering one’s ignorance each time one learns’), so is kāmam (love) each time he draws close (ceṟitōṟum) to the cēyiḻai (சேயிழை, ‘she of red, i.e. gold, jewels’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah specify learning from books (nūl), and Solomon Pappaiah reads the second half as love’s savour appearing ever new; Kalaignar likewise has ‘knowing new things again and again’. The verse links the Kamattuppal to the Porutpal chapters on learning (ch. 40-43), and turns the humility of the scholar into a picture of inexhaustible love. Pope’s second line slightly shifts the sense: ‘The more men learn, the more their lack of learning they detect; / ’Tis so when I approach the maid with gleaming jewels decked.’ The ytamizh.com ‘Couplet Explanation’ reads it as repeated union only creating desire for more, a narrower gloss than the Tamil commentators give. Text identical on both source sites.

tamil:
நன்னீரை வாழி அனிச்சமே நின்னினும்
மென்னீரள் யாம்வீழ் பவள்.
transliteration:
Nanneerai vaazhi anichchamae ninninum
menneeral yaamveezh paval.
current_meaning: Bless you, anicham flower, you are delicate indeed; but the one I love is more delicate still than you.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you hold the softest feather you have ever found and say, 'You are so soft!' Then you remember your baby sister's cheek and smile: 'But she is even softer.' The poet does the same with the softest flower he knows.
university_explanation: Chapter 112 belongs to the kalaviyal (the section on secret, premarital love) and follows ch. 111 (Punarchi Magizhthal, the joy of union): the hero now 'adorns in words' (punainthu uraiththal) the nalam (நலம், 'goodness, loveliness') of the heroine, a stock situation of Tamil akam poetry. The anicham (அனிச்சம்) is the proverbial most delicate flower in Tamil, said to wilt merely when smelled (cf. Kural 90, மோப்பக் குழையும் அனிச்சம்), and nanneerai (நன்னீரை, 'you are of fine nature') with the blessing vaazhi ('may you flourish') makes the flower a polite rival before it is surpassed by the beloved's men-neer (மென்னீர், 'softer nature'). In the line of Parimelazhagar the hero speaks this aside after union, praising what he has just experienced; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as 'my beloved is softer than you'. Pope renders: 'O flower of the sensitive plant! than thee / More tender's the maiden beloved by me.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மலர்காணின் மையாத்தி நெஞ்சே இவள்கண்
பலர்காணும் பூவொக்கும் என்று.
transliteration:
Malarkaanin maiyaaththi nenjae ivalkan
palarkaanum poovokkum endru.
current_meaning: My heart, you grow giddy whenever you see flowers, thinking her eyes are like these blossoms that anyone can look at; but they are not.
elementary_explanation: Suppose your best friend has a special smile. Whenever you see a smiley sticker, you think, 'That looks like my friend!' and get excited. Then you laugh at yourself: a sticker anyone can buy is nothing like the real smile.
university_explanation: The hero addresses his own nenju (நெஞ்சு, 'heart'), a common device in Tamil love poetry, and scolds it for its confusion (மையாத்தல், maiyaaththal, 'to be bewildered'). The flowers in question are taken by the commentators as kuvalai (குவளை, blue water-lily), the standard comparison for dark eyes; Puliyur Kesikan names the kuvalai explicitly. The sting is in palar kaanum (பலர் காணும், 'seen by many'): common flowers that every passer-by may look at cannot resemble eyes that he alone beholds, which Solomon Pappaiah brings out ('the eyes of my wife whom I alone see'); Kalaignar instead reads it as 'her eyes are a flower that many marvel at', a minority interpretation. Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes the verse as the hero rejecting the conventional comparison as unworthy. Pope: 'You deemed, as you saw the flowers, her eyes were as flowers, my soul, / That many may see.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
முறிமேனி முத்தம் முறுவல் வெறிநாற்றம்
வேலுண்கண் வேய்த்தோ ளவட்கு.
transliteration:
Murimaeni muththam muruval verinaatram
vaelunkan vaeyththo lavatku.
current_meaning: She whose shoulders are like bamboo has a body the colour of tender leaves, a smile of pearls, a natural fragrance, and kohl-darkened eyes sharp as lances.
elementary_explanation: This is like drawing a picture of someone you love using things from nature: new green leaves for skin, shiny pearls for teeth, a flower-garden smell, and smooth bamboo for shoulders. Every part gets its own beautiful match.
university_explanation: This kural is a compact catalogue of the heroine’s features, each paired with its classical Tamil upamaanam (standard of comparison): muri (முறி, tender sprout, esp. of mango) for her complexion, muththam (முத்தம், pearl) for her smiling teeth (muruval), veri naatram (வெறி நாற்றம், natural fragrance, not applied scent) for her body’s scent, vel (வேல், lance) for her un-kan (உண்கண், kohl-'eaten' eyes) and vey (வேய், bamboo) for her rounded shoulders. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan all parse it as 'for her of bamboo shoulders: tender shoot is the body, pearl the teeth, fragrance the scent, lance the eyes', which is the Parimelazhagar construction; Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads muththam as 'kiss', an outlier. The printed division 'வேய்த்தோ ளவட்கு' (ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net) is a metrical split of வேய்த்தோள் அவட்கு and not a variant. Pope: 'As tender shoot her frame; teeth, pearls; around her odours blend; / Darts are the eyes of her whose shoulders like the bambu bend.'

tamil:
காணின் குவளை கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்
மாணிழை கண்ணொவ்வேம் என்று.
transliteration:
Kaanin kuvalai kavizhndhu nilannoakkum
maanizhai kannovvaem endru.
current_meaning: If the blue water-lilies could see her, they would hang their heads and stare at the ground, saying, 'We cannot match the eyes of this finely adorned one.'
elementary_explanation: Picture the prettiest flowers in a garden suddenly able to see. They look at a girl’s lovely eyes, feel shy, and droop their heads, as if saying, 'We can’t compete with that!'
university_explanation: The conceit (a form of what later poetics calls tharkurippetram, attributing a feeling to something that has none) gives the kuvalai (குவளை, blue water-lily, the stock comparison for eyes) the power of sight and shame: it would kavizhndhu nilan nokkum (கவிழ்ந்து நிலன் நோக்கும், 'bend down and look at the ground'), the gesture of a defeated or abashed person. The botanical observation behind it is that the kuvalai flower droops on its stalk. Maanizhai (மாணிழை, 'she of excellent jewels') is a standard epithet for the heroine. Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah agree on the sense; Pappaiah adds 'out of shame' (நாணத்தால்). In the Parimelazhagar tradition this kural follows 1112 as its answer: the flower itself knows it cannot match her eyes. Pope (who translates kuvalai as 'lotus'): 'The lotus, seeing her, with head demiss, the ground would eye.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அனிச்சப்பூக் கால்களையாள் பெய்தாள் நுகப்பிற்கு
நல்ல படாஅ பறை.
transliteration:
Anichchappook kaalkalaiyaal peydhaal nukappirku
nalla pataaa parai.
current_meaning: She has worn anicham flowers without removing their stems; for her slender waist, no happy drums will sound now.
elementary_explanation: This is a funny exaggeration, like saying, 'She is so light that one extra feather in her hair might tip her over!' The poet pretends her waist is so delicate that even tiny flower stems are too heavy for it.
university_explanation: A deliberate hyperbole (உயர்வு நவிற்சி): the heroine has put anicham flowers in her hair kaal kalaiyaal (கால் களையாள், 'without plucking off the stalks'), and the poet pretends that the weight of those tiny stalks will break her nukappu (நுகப்பு, waist). Nalla padaa parai (நல்ல படாஅ பறை, with the metrical lengthening படாஅ) means 'drums that are good will not sound', i.e. only the drums of mourning, not festive drums; this is the reading of Parimelazhagar’s tradition followed by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, while Solomon Pappaiah glosses parai as 'auspicious sounds'. Kalaignar narrates it as already happened ('her waist has broken'), a dramatised variant of the same sense. Pope’s version alters the scene to a girdle of flowers: 'The flowers of the sensitive plant as a girdle around her she placed; / The stems she forgot to nip off; they’ll weigh down the delicate waist.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மதியும் மடந்தை முகனும் அறியா
பதியின் கலங்கிய மீன்.
transliteration:
Madhiyum madandhai mukanum ariyaa
padhiyin kalangiya meen.
current_meaning: Unable to tell the moon from this young woman’s face, the stars have been thrown into confusion and wander from their places.
elementary_explanation: Imagine the stars as a class of children who always stand near their teacher, the moon. One night a girl with a face as bright as the moon walks by, and the stars get mixed up: 'Which one is our moon?' They start running about in a muddle.
university_explanation: A cosmic hyperbole: the meen (மீன், stars; literally 'fish', the common Tamil word for stars) cannot tell madhi (மதி, moon) from the madandhai’s (மடந்தை, young woman’s) mukan (முகன், face) and are kalangiya (கலங்கிய, 'agitated, confused') in their pathi (பதி, 'fixed station'). In the Parimelazhagar tradition the stars, which in Indian astronomy move in fixed relation to the moon through the lunar mansions (naksatra), are thrown out of their courses by seeing two moons. All the modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesikan) agree on 'the stars are troubled and leave their places'. This kural opens a run of four (1116-1119) built on the moon-and-face comparison. Pope: 'The stars perplexed are rushing wildly from their spheres; / For like another moon this maiden’s face appears.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அறுவாய் நிறைந்த அவிர்மதிக்குப் போல
மறுவுண்டோ மாதர் முகத்து.
transliteration:
Aruvaai niraindha avirmadhikkup poala
maruvundoa maadhar mukaththu.
current_meaning: The bright moon fills out again after waning, yet it carries a dark spot; is there any such blemish on this woman’s face?
elementary_explanation: The moon is lovely, but if you look closely you can see dark patches on it. The poet looks at his beloved’s face and says, 'The moon has spots, but her face has none at all.'
university_explanation: This kural answers the confusion of 1116: why should the stars be confused, when the face differs from the moon? Aruvaai niraindha (அறுவாய் நிறைந்த, 'whose cut-away parts have filled up') describes the moon that waxes after waning, and avir madhi (அவிர் மதி, 'shining moon') its full splendour; yet the moon has a maru (மறு, 'blemish, spot', the dark marks traditionally seen as a hare), which the woman’s face lacks. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan make the link with 1116 explicit ('why should the stars be troubled?'); Sivayogi Sivakumar reads maru as 'change', an outlier gloss. The rhetorical question (வினா) carries the force of denial, as in Parimelazhagar’s construal. Pope: 'In moon, that waxing waning shines, as spots appear, / Are any spots discerned in face of maiden here?' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மாதர் முகம்போல் ஒளிவிட வல்லையேல்
காதலை வாழி மதி.
transliteration:
Maadhar mukampoal olivida vallaiyael
kaadhalai vaazhi madhi.
current_meaning: Long may you live, moon! If you could shine like this woman’s face, you too would win my love.
elementary_explanation: It is like telling the moon, 'You’re nice, Moon, but if you could glow as brightly as my best friend’s happy face, then I’d love you too!'
university_explanation: The hero now speaks to the moon directly (an apostrophe, as to the anicham in 1111), blessing it with vaazhi (வாழி, 'may you flourish') and offering a conditional: vallaiyel (வல்லையேல், 'if you are able') to shine (oli vida) like her face, kaadhalai (காதலை, 'you would be one beloved', the verbal noun as predicate) by him. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan: 'you too would earn my love as she does'; Solomon Pappaiah: 'if you shine so that I rejoice, you would win my love'; Kalaignar reads it rather differently, as advice to the moon to shine like her face if it wants to be loved. The playful implication, as Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes it, is that the moon cannot meet the condition. Pope: 'Farewell, O moon! If that thine orb could shine / Bright as her face, thou shouldst be love of mine.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மலரன்ன கண்ணாள் முகமொத்தி யாயின்
பலர்காணத் தோன்றல் மதி.
transliteration:
Malaranna kannaal mukamoththi yaayin
palarkaanath thoandral madhi.
current_meaning: Moon, if you wish to be like the face of her whose eyes are like flowers, do not appear where everyone can see you.
elementary_explanation: Think of a special treasure you keep in a box just for yourself. The poet tells the moon: 'If you want to be as special as her face, don’t show yourself to everyone. Her face is like a treasure only I get to see.'
university_explanation: The moon sequence closes with a second condition: if the moon is to resemble (oththi, ஒத்தி, 'you resemble') the face of malaranna kannaal (மலரன்ன கண்ணாள், 'she whose eyes are like flowers'), it must not appear palar kaana (பலர் காண, 'for many to see'), since her face is seen by him alone. The idea picks up palar kaanum ('seen by many') from 1112, and Solomon Pappaiah draws the link: 'appear for me alone, not for all to see'. Kalaignar reads it as advice to the moon to stay hidden so as not to lose the comparison; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan give the plain prohibition. The exclusivity reflects the kalavu (secret love) setting, in which the heroine is unseen by others. Pope: 'If as her face, whose eyes are flowers, thou wouldst have charms for me, / Shine for my eyes alone, O moon, shine not for all to see!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அனிச்சமும் அன்னத்தின் தூவியும் மாதர்
அடிக்கு நெருஞ்சிப் பழம்.
transliteration:
Anichchamum annaththin thooviyum maadhar
atikku nerunjip pazham.
current_meaning: Even the anicham flower and the swan’s soft down feel like thorny caltrop burrs to this woman’s feet.
elementary_explanation: Imagine feet so tender that walking on a fluffy cotton ball feels like stepping on a prickly burr. That is how gently the poet imagines his beloved, as a playful, loving exaggeration.
university_explanation: The chapter ends as it began, with the anicham (1111), now joined by the annaththin thuvi (அன்னத்தின் தூவி, the swan’s down), the two classical standards of softness; both are said to be nerunjip pazham (நெருஞ்சிப் பழம், the spiny fruit of the caltrop, Tribulus terrestris) to her adi (அடி, feet). The figure is a hyperbole of delicacy in which the softest things become sharp; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'like nerunji thorns', Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan 'they cause pain as the nerunji fruit does'. Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes pazham here as the ripe, hardened fruit with its spines. Some commentators take maadhar as women in general, others (Pappaiah, Kalaignar) as the speaker’s own beloved; the context of the chapter supports the latter. Pope: 'The flower of the sensitive plant, and the down on the swan’s white breast, / As the thorn are harsh, by the delicate feet of this maiden pressed.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பாலொடு தேன்கலந் தற்றே பணிமொழி
வாலெயிறு ஊறிய நீர்.
transliteration:
Paalodu thaenkalandh thatrae panimozhi
vaaleyiru ooriya neer.
current_meaning: The moisture on the white teeth of this softly spoken girl is like milk and honey mixed together.
elementary_explanation: Think of the sweetest drink you can imagine, warm milk with a spoon of honey stirred in. The poet says that being close to the person he loves feels that sweet. It is his way of saying that love makes everything about the beloved seem delightful.
university_explanation: Chapter 113 belongs to the kalaviyal (the section on secret, premarital love) and opens with the hero speaking after union, declaring the special excellence (sirappu) of the love itself rather than of the beloved's looks, which was the topic of ch. 112. Pani-mozhi (பணிமொழி, 'gentle, deferential speech') names the heroine by her soft voice, and vaal-eyiru (வாலெயிறு, 'white teeth') is a stock feature of the akam heroine; ooriya neer ('the water that wells up') is a decorous image for the sweetness of a kiss. Milk-and-honey (paalodu thaen) is the classical Tamil figure for perfect sweetness; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss the line this way, Pope renders 'The dew on her white teeth, whose voice is soft and low, / Is as when milk and honey mingled flow', and the commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar reads the chapter's first five couplets as the hero's words. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்னமற் றன்ன
மடந்தையொடு எம்மிடை நட்பு.
transliteration:
Udambodu uyiridai ennamat ranna
madandhaiyodu emmidai natpu.
current_meaning: Whatever the bond is between body and life, such is the bond between this young woman and me.
elementary_explanation: Your body and the life inside it always go together; you can't send one to school and leave the other at home. The poet says he and the person he loves belong together in that same way.
university_explanation: The hero now states the inseparability of the lovers through the classic Indian pairing of udambu (உடம்பு, body) and uyir (உயிர், life or soul). The word chosen for the relationship is natpu (நட்பு, 'friendship, intimacy'), the same term that heads the Porutpaal chapters on friendship (ch. 79 onward), so the love is presented as a perfect friendship. Madandhai (மடந்தை) denotes a young woman, conventionally of marriageable age. Modern commentators agree on the sense: Mu. Varadarasanar ('as the ties between body and life'), Solomon Pappaiah ('the relation between body and life'), Kalaignar ('life and body never live apart; such is our relationship'); Pope translates 'Between this maid and me the friendship kind / Is as the bonds that soul and body bind.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கருமணியிற் பாவாய்நீ போதாயாம் வீழும்
திருநுதற்கு இல்லை இடம்.
transliteration:
Karumaniyir paavaainee poadhaayaam veezhum
thirunudharku illai idam.
current_meaning: O little image in the pupil of my eye, go away; there is no room there for the fair-browed one I love.
elementary_explanation: When you look closely into someone's eye you can see a tiny picture of yourself in it. The poet tells that tiny picture to move out, because he wants his eye to hold only the person he loves.
university_explanation: The conceit rests on paavai (பாவை, 'doll, image'), the tiny reflected figure visible in the karumani (கருமணி, the dark pupil); the lover orders it to leave (poadhaai) because there is no idam (இடம், 'room') for thiru-nudhal (திருநுதல், 'she of the lovely brow'), a standard epithet for the heroine. The idea is that he wants to hold her image permanently in his sight. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree; Pope: 'For her with beauteous brow, the maid I love, there place is none; / To give her image room, O pupil of mine eye, begone!' Pulavar Kesikan's gloss adds 'there is no other place for her to stay', heightening the hyperbole. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கன்னள் ஆயிழை சாதல்
அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து.
transliteration:
Vaazhdhal uyirkkannal aayizhai saadhal
adharkannal neengum idaththu.
current_meaning: My finely jewelled love is like life to my soul when she is with me, and like death to it when she leaves.
elementary_explanation: When your best friend is with you the whole day feels bright, and when they go home it can feel empty and dark. The poet says the person he loves feels like life itself when near, and leaving feels like losing life.
university_explanation: The couplet balances vaazhdhal (வாழ்தல், living) against saadhal (சாதல், dying), with annal (அன்னள், 'she is like') repeated in each half and neengum idaththu ('at the time she departs') as the hinge. Aayizhai (ஆயிழை) is an epithet, 'she of chosen jewels'; Kalaignar extends it to 'she who wears chosen virtues as her ornaments'. Mu. Varadarasanar: 'when she joins me she is like life to my soul, when she parts she is like death to it'; Solomon Pappaiah reads the first half as 'like the body to the soul', a slightly different construal of the same syntax. Pope: 'Life is she to my very soul when she draws nigh; / Dissevered from the maid with jewels rare, I die!' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் மறப்பின் மறப்பறியேன்
ஒள்ளமர்க் கண்ணாள் குணம்.
transliteration:
Ulluvan manyaan marappin marappariyaen
ollamark kannaal gunam.
current_meaning: If I ever forgot the qualities of the girl with bright, battling eyes, I could remember them; but I never forget them at all.
elementary_explanation: You only need to remember something if you have forgotten it. The poet says he never needs to remember the girl he loves, because she is never out of his mind for a moment.
university_explanation: The paradox turns on ulluvan (உள்ளுவன், 'I would recall') against marappu ariyaen (மறப்பறியேன், 'I do not know forgetting'): recollection presupposes forgetting, and since he never forgets her, he never has to 'remember' her. The particle man (மன்) marks the conditional as unrealised. Ol-amar-kannaal (ஒள்ளமர்க் கண்ணாள்) is read two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Pope take amar as 'battle', hence 'bright, warring eyes' (Pope: 'whose eyes gleam like the warrior's dart'), while Pulavar Kesikan reads ollivaai amarndha, 'bright and calmly set'. Pope's note, following the commentators, says the hero speaks to the heroine's maid (tozhi), who had asked whether he still remembered her. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார் இமைப்பின் பருகுவரா
நுண்ணியர்எம் காத லவர்.
transliteration:
Kannullin poakaar imaippin paruguvaraa
nunniyarem kaadha lavar.
current_meaning: My lover never leaves my eyes, and even when I blink he is not hurt, so subtle and fine is he.
elementary_explanation: Imagine keeping a picture of someone you love in your mind so clearly that it stays even when you blink. Blinking can't hurt that picture because it is not made of anything solid. The girl in this poem says her love lives in her eyes like that.
university_explanation: With this couplet the voice passes to the heroine (talaivi), who answers her companion's worry that the hero is far away: he is always in her eyes. Kannullin poagaar (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார், 'he does not leave from within my eyes') is followed by imaippin paruguvaraa (இமைப்பின் பருகுவரா, 'he does not suffer if I blink'), and nunniyar (நுண்ணியர், 'subtle, fine') explains why: he is too fine to be crushed by the eyelids. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pulavar Kesikan and Kalaignar all read paruguvaraa as 'will not be pained'; Solomon Pappaiah adds that 'others cannot perceive his subtle nature'. Pope takes it differently, 'I wink them not, lest I should pain him where he lies', which anticipates the not-blinking motif of 1129. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கண்ணுள்ளார் காத லவராகக் கண்ணும்
எழுதேம் கரப்பாக்கு அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Kannullaar kaadha lavaraagak kannum
ezhudhaem karappaakku arindhu.
current_meaning: Because my lover lives in my eyes, I do not even line them with kohl, knowing it would hide him.
elementary_explanation: If you were keeping a tiny friend inside a glass jar, you wouldn't paint the jar, because then you couldn't see them. The girl in this poem doesn't put on eye makeup because she imagines her love is inside her eyes and the makeup would cover him.
university_explanation: The heroine continues the eye conceit: since her lover dwells in her eyes (kannullaar), she will not even 'write' her eyes (kannum ezhudhaem), ezhudhu (எழுது) being the Tamil verb for applying mai (மை, kohl or collyrium), for fear of karappu (கரப்பு, concealment) of him. Applying kohl was a basic daily adornment of the akam heroine, so giving it up shows how completely her life is ordered around him. The umm in kannum ('even the eyes') implies she forgoes other adornment too. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree on 'lest he be hidden'; Pope: 'My love doth ever in my eyes reside; / I stain them not, fearing his form to hide.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நெஞ்சத்தார் காத லவராக வெய்துண்டல்
அஞ்சுதும் வேபாக் கறிந்து.
transliteration:
Nenjaththaar kaadha lavaraaga veydhundal
anjudhum vaepaak karindhu.
current_meaning: Because my lover lives in my heart, I am afraid to eat anything hot, knowing it would burn him.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever carried a baby bird very carefully so it wouldn't get hurt? The girl in this poem feels her love is living right inside her chest, so she won't even drink something hot in case it burns him.
university_explanation: The conceit moves from the eyes to the heart: nenjaththaar (நெஞ்சத்தார், 'he who is in my heart') is so literally present that veydhu undal (வெய்துண்டல், eating hot food) is feared (anjudhum, அஞ்சுதும்) because of vaepaakku (வேபாக்கு, his being scorched). The first person plural is the heroine's dignified 'we'. All four commentators on thirukkural.net and ytamizh.com agree on the sense; Kalaignar generalises it into a definition: true lovers are those so blended heart with heart that they fear hot food might burn the other. Pope: 'Within my heart my lover dwells; from food I turn / That smacks of heat, lest he should feel it burn.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல் அனைத்திற்கே
ஏதிலர் என்னும்இவ் வூர்.
transliteration:
Imaippin karappaakku arival anaiththirkae
aedhilar ennumiv voor.
current_meaning: I know that if I blink he will be hidden, so I keep my eyes open; and for that alone this town calls him unloving.
elementary_explanation: Suppose you stayed up late because you were thinking about someone you love, and the next day people said, 'That person must be unkind to keep you awake!' The girl in this poem says the town blames her lover, though really it is just her love that keeps her eyes open.
university_explanation: The heroine explains her sleeplessness: she will not close her eyes because she knows that on blinking (imaippin) he would be hidden (karappaakku). Seeing her wakeful and pale, the ur (ஊர், 'town') concludes that he is aedhilar (ஏதிலர், 'a stranger, one without love') who has abandoned her, and she protests the injustice. Anaiththirkae ('for just that much') marks the town's verdict as unfair. This introduces alar (அலர், gossip), the theme of ch. 115. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pulavar Kesikan agree; Kalaignar adds that the town blames him for the 'pain of sleeplessness'. Pope: 'I fear his form to hide, nor close my eyes: / "Her love estranged is gone!" the village cries.' The second line is shared verbatim with 1130, a deliberate refrain. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும் இகந்துறைவர்
ஏதிலர் என்னும்இவ் வூர்.
transliteration:
Uvandhuraivar ullaththul endrum igandhuraivar
aedhilar ennumiv voor.
current_meaning: He lives happily in my heart always, yet this town says he lives far away and does not love me.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes people only see what is on the outside. Someone might think two friends have drifted apart because they live in different places, but the friends know they still care about each other every day. The girl in this poem says her love is always in her heart, even if the town thinks he is gone.
university_explanation: The chapter closes by contrasting uvandhu uraivar (உவந்துறைவர், 'he dwells rejoicing') ullaththul endrum ('in my heart always') with the town's verdict that he igandhu uraivar (இகந்துறைவர், 'lives having gone away') and is aedhilar, unloving. The repetition of uraivar and the refrain line shared with 1129 sharpen the irony: physical distance is visible to the town, but inner presence is visible only to her. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pulavar Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree; Pope: 'Rejoicing in my very soul he ever lies; / "Her love estranged is gone far off!" the village cries.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காமம் உழந்து வருந்தினார்க்கு ஏமம்
மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி.
transliteration:
Kaamam uzhandhu varundhinaarkku Emam
madalalladhu illai vali.
current_meaning: For those who have known love and now suffer because it is denied them, there is no protection and no strength left except riding the palm-stem horse (madal) in public.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a boy who has asked and asked for something important and been told no every time. At last he decides to make a big, brave sign and carry it through the whole village so everyone knows how much it matters to him. In old Tamil stories, a young man who was kept away from the girl he loved could do something like this: ride a pretend horse made of palm leaves down the street.
university_explanation: Chapter 114 opens with the custom of madal ūrtal (மடல் ஊர்தல்): a lover refused access to his beloved would ride a hobby-horse made of palmyra stems (madal) through the streets, garlanded with erukkam flowers and carrying her likeness, to shame her family publicly into consenting; Kalittokai and Tolkāppiyam know the practice, and the grammatical tradition classes it as an extreme of love (peruntiṇai). Ēmam (ஏமம்) means 'safeguard, refuge' and vali (வலி) 'strength, support'; uḻantu (உழந்து) is 'having laboured/suffered in'. In the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar the opening couplets are the hero's words to the heroine's confidante (tōḻi) when she puts him off, and the threat of the madal is itself a way of abandoning nāṇ (நாண், 'shame, reserve'), which gives the chapter its name. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss the line as 'no strength but the madal'; Pope renders 'Except the helpful horse of palm, no other strength remains.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நோனா உடம்பும் உயிரும் மடலேறும்
நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து.
transliteration:
Nonaa udambum uyirum madalaerum
naaninai neekki niruththu.
current_meaning: My body and my life, unable to bear this any longer, have put shame aside and are ready to mount the palm-stem horse.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever been so upset that you cried in front of everyone, even though you usually would feel shy? The speaker here says his whole body and heart are hurting so much that his shyness has simply been set aside.
university_explanation: Nōṉā (நோனா) is the negative participle of nōl, 'to endure': the body and the life-breath (uyir) that 'cannot bear' the separation are made the subjects of the verb, as if they act on their own. Nāṇiṉai nīkki niṟuttu (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து), 'having removed and set aside shame', is the key phrase of the chapter: nāṇ, the sense of reserve that Tamil ethics praises (cf. chapter 102, Nāṇuṭaimai), is not destroyed but deliberately put to one side. Commentators in Parimelazhagar's line take this as the hero telling the confidante that his resolve is already made; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'my body and life have resolved to ride the madal, having set shame aside', while Pappaiah softens it to 'are thinking of riding'. Pope: 'My body and my soul, that can no more endure, / Will lay reserve aside, and mount the horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன் இன்றுடையேன்
காமுற்றார் ஏறும் மடல்.
transliteration:
Naanodu nallaanmai pandudaiyaen indrudaiyaen
kaamutraar aerum madal.
current_meaning: Once I had modesty and honourable manliness; today all I have is the palm-stem horse that love-stricken men ride.
elementary_explanation: Think of a proud, well-behaved prince who always acted with dignity. Then he falls so deeply in love that he will do anything, even something silly in front of everyone, to be heard. He says, 'I used to be so proper; now look at me!'
university_explanation: The couplet sets paṇṭu (பண்டு, 'formerly') against iṉṟu (இன்று, 'today'), and nāṇ (நாண், 'modesty, sense of shame') together with nal-āṇmai (நல்லாண்மை, 'good manliness, honourable valour') against the single possession now left, the madal. Parimelazhagar's tradition reads this as the hero's lament that love has stripped him of the two qualities that defined him socially. Kāmuṟṟār (காமுற்றார்) is 'those seized by love'; the madal is thus marked as the emblem of a class of sufferers rather than a personal eccentricity. Pope: 'I once retained reserve and seemly manliness; / To-day I nought possess but lovers' horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும் நாணொடு
நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை.
transliteration:
Kaamak kadumpunal uykkum naanodu
nallaanmai ennum punai.
current_meaning: The fierce flood of love sweeps away the raft made of modesty and honourable manliness.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you are floating safely on a little raft. Then a huge flood rushes in and carries the raft away. The poet says love is like that flood, and being careful and well-behaved is the raft it sweeps off.
university_explanation: The image is a rūpakam (extended metaphor): kāmak kaṭum-puṉal (காமக் கடும்புனல்), 'the fierce torrent of love', against puṇai (புணை), a raft or float, which here is made of two things, nāṇ (modesty) and nal-āṇmai (honourable manliness), both named in the previous couplet. Uykkum (உய்க்கும்) means 'carries off, drives along'. Commentators (Parimelazhagar's line, Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah) all take it as the hero's explanation of why the qualities he once had could not save him; Puliyur Kesikan adds an exclamation, 'what shall I do!'. Pope: 'Love's rushing tide will sweep away the raft / Of seemly manliness and shame combined.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தொடலைக் குறுந்தொடி தந்தாள் மடலொடு
மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்.
transliteration:
Thodalaik kurundhodi thandhaal madalodu
maalai uzhakkum thuyar.
current_meaning: She who wears small bangles strung like a garland has given me both the palm-stem horse and the sorrow that torments me every evening.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes a person we like very much can make us feel happy and sad at the same time. The speaker says the girl with the pretty little bangles has given him two things: a heavy heart every evening, and the idea of riding the palm horse.
university_explanation: Toṭalaik kuṟun-toṭi (தொடலைக் குறுந்தொடி) is an epithet standing for the heroine: 'she of the small bangles (kuṟun-toṭi) that are like a garland or string (toṭalai)'. Commentators differ on toṭalai: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as 'garland-like, continuous', Kesikan as 'a linked set', while Kalaignar reads in a girdle (mēkalai) as well; Pappaiah's text appears to read 'like a mountain' (malai pōla), probably a misprint for mālai. Mālai uḻakkum tuyar (மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்), 'the sorrow that harrows in the evening', invokes the akam convention that evening is the hardest hour for separated lovers. Pope: 'The maid that slender armlets wears, like flowers entwined, / Has brought me horse of palm, and pangs of eventide!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மடலூர்தல் யாமத்தும் உள்ளுவேன் மன்ற
படல்ஒல்லா பேதைக்கென் கண்.
transliteration:
Madaloordhal yaamaththum ulluvaen mandra
padalollaa paedhaikken kan.
current_meaning: Even at midnight I think about riding the palm-stem horse, for my eyes will not close in sleep because of that innocent girl.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever been so worried or excited that you couldn't fall asleep? The speaker lies awake in the middle of the night, thinking about the girl he loves and about his big plan to tell the whole village.
university_explanation: Yāmam (யாமம்) is the deep watch of the night, midnight; uḷḷuvēṉ (உள்ளுவேன்) 'I shall think, brood on', with maṉṟa (மன்ற) 'certainly' as an intensifier. Paṭal ollā (படல் ஒல்லா), 'not consenting to close', describes eyes that will not shut, and pētai (பேதை), literally 'innocent, simple one', is a conventional endearment for the heroine (also a technical term for the youngest of the seven stages of womanhood). Commentators in Parimelazhagar's line take it as the hero assuring the confidante that his resolve is not a passing mood but something he dwells on even at midnight. The ytamizh.com text prints படல்ஒல்லா without a space, thirukkural.net the same; editions vary only in spacing. Pope: 'Of climbing horse of palm in midnight hour, I think; / My eyes know no repose for that same simple maid.'

tamil:
கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும் மடலேறாப்
பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க தில்.
transliteration:
Kadalanna kaamam uzhandhum madalaeraap
pennin perundhakka thil.
current_meaning: There is nothing nobler than a woman who, though she suffers a love as vast as the sea, never rides the palm-stem horse.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two friends who both miss someone very much. One shouts about it all over town; the other keeps going quietly and patiently. The poet says the quiet, patient strength the woman shows is one of the greatest things in the world.
university_explanation: The couplet turns the chapter: kaṭal aṉṉa kāmam (கடலன்ன காமம்), 'love like the sea', is borne (uḻantum, 'even while suffering') by the woman who nonetheless does not ride the madal (maṭal ēṟā). This echoes the Tolkāppiyam rule that the madal is never proper for women, and the commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it as praise of the endurance of women; Kesikan sharpens it into a comparison: no man has such worth. The speaker is disputed: some commentators give it to the hero, conceding the heroine's greater restraint, while others read it as the heroine's own words, and many hear the remaining couplets of the chapter in her voice. Perun-takkatu il (பெருந்தக்கது இல்) is 'there is nothing of greater worth'. Pope: 'There's nought of greater worth than woman's long-enduring soul, / Who, vexed by love like ocean waves, climbs not the horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நிறையரியர் மன்அளியர் என்னாது காமம்
மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்.
transliteration:
Niraiyariyar manaliyar ennaadhu kaamam
maraiyirandhu mandru padum.
current_meaning: Love does not stop to consider whether someone is restrained or deserving of pity; it breaks out of its secrecy and shows itself in the public square.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever tried to keep a happy secret, but your big smile gave it away? Love can be like that. Even when someone tries very hard to hide it, it shows on their face and everyone in town finds out.
university_explanation: The key words are niṟai (நிறை), 'firmness of mind, the power to keep one's feelings in', aḷiyar (அளியர்), 'those deserving pity', maṟai (மறை), 'secrecy', and maṉṟu (மன்று), the village common or public assembly ground where talk spreads. The opening phrase niṟai-ariyar is read in two opposite ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it as 'lacking restraint', while Solomon Pappaiah reads 'very restrained' (ariyar as 'hard to overcome'), and Pope follows the second ('In virtue hard to move, yet very tender, too, are we'). Pope's 'we' reflects the common view that from here the heroine is speaking, lamenting that her love is about to become public gossip (alar), which leads into chapter 115. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அறிகிலார் எல்லாரும் என்றேஎன் காமம்
மறுகின் மறுகும் மருண்டு.
transliteration:
Arikilaar ellaarum endrae-en kaamam
marukin marukum marundu.
current_meaning: As if thinking that not everyone knows of it yet, my love wanders bewildered through the streets.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a puppy that has escaped from its yard and runs up and down the street, bumping into everyone. The speaker says her love is like that: it has got out and is wandering around town where everyone can see it.
university_explanation: Love itself is personified: thinking 'not everyone knows' (aṟikilār ellārum), it maṟukiṉ maṟukum (மறுகின் மறுகும்), 'roams about in the street', maruṇṭu (மருண்டு), 'in confusion, bewildered'. The pun on maṟuku (street) and maṟukum (wanders, whirls) is characteristic of Valluvar's sound-play. Commentators note the irony: because the speaker had kept quiet (Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar: 'because I endured in silence'), love itself seems to have decided to announce itself; Pappaiah says it goes about the streets as gossip (ampal and alar), anticipating chapter 115. The ytamizh.com text prints என்றேஎன் as one unit and thirukkural.net the same; Pope reads 'There's no one knows my heart, so says my love'.

tamil:
யாம்கண்ணின் காண நகுப அறிவில்லார்
யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு.
transliteration:
Yaamkannin kaana nagupa arivillaar
yaampatta thaampadaa aaru.
current_meaning: Thoughtless people laugh at me right before my eyes, only because they have never suffered what I suffer.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever seen someone laugh at a friend who was crying, just because they didn't understand how sad the friend felt? The speaker says people who laugh at lovers only do it because they have never felt that pain themselves.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a balanced contrast: yām paṭṭa (யாம் பட்ட), 'what I have suffered', against tām paṭā (தாம் படா), 'what they have not suffered', with āṟu (ஆறு), 'the manner, the reason', at the end. Aṟivillār (அறிவில்லார்), 'those without understanding', laugh kaṇṇiṉ kāṇa (கண்ணின் காண), 'so that I see it with my eyes', that is, openly to the speaker's face. Commentators take it as the closing lament of the chapter, spoken in the tradition as the heroine's words once her love is known, and Kalaignar turns it into a general maxim: only those who have never known love's pain mock its sufferers. Pope: 'Before my eyes the foolish make a mock of me, / Because they ne'er endured the pangs I now must drie.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும் அதனைப்
பலரறியார் பாக்கியத் தால்.
transliteration:
alarezha aaruyir niRkum adhanaip
palaraRiyaar paakkiyath thaal
current_meaning: Now that the town is gossiping about our love, my precious life, which was ebbing away, holds on; by good fortune the gossips do not realise that their talk is what keeps me alive.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you have a secret friend you are not allowed to play with, and you feel very sad. Then the other children start teasing, ‘You two are best friends!’ Strangely, the teasing makes you feel better, because now everyone treats you as a pair. The young man in this verse feels just like that, and he is glad the teasers have not worked out that they are helping him.
university_explanation: Chapter 115, alar aṟivuṟuttal (அலர் அறிவுறுத்தல்), concerns alar (அலர்) and its synonym kauvai (கௌவை), the village gossip that breaks out once a secret courtship (kaḷavu) becomes known; Parimelazhagar’s preface says the chapter has the hero telling the confidante (tōḻi) how the rumour serves him, and the heroine and tōḻi telling the hero of it to press him toward marriage (varaivu) or elopement (uṭanpōkku), and that it follows the chapter on abandoning reserve because it arises once nāṇ is given up. Parimelazhagar sets this couplet as the hero’s reply when the tōḻi, after a failed tryst, uses the rumour to urge marriage: the rumour makes the hard-to-win girl seem attainable, so his ‘precious life’ (ār uyir) has a support (paṟṟukkōṭu); pākkiyam (பாக்கியம்) is glossed teyvam, ‘fate, providence’, which keeps the gossips from realising this, for if they knew they would fall silent and his life would go. Manakkudavar instead reads ār uyir as the heroine’s life. The text is identical on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com; Pope renders ‘By this same rumour’s rise, my precious life stands fast.’

tamil:
மலரன்ன கண்ணாள் அருமை அறியாது
அலரெமக்கு ஈந்ததிவ் வூர்.
transliteration:
malaranna kaNNaaL arumai aRiyaadhu
alaremakku eendhadhiv voor
current_meaning: Not knowing how rare and hard to win is the girl with flower-like eyes, this town has handed me a rumour linking us, and so has done me a favour.
elementary_explanation: Suppose there is a very special girl in your class whom everyone thinks is out of reach. One day people start saying, ‘Oh, she likes you!’ They are only gossiping, but the gossip makes her seem a little closer. The young man in this verse thanks the town for gossiping, because the town has no idea how precious she really is.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar marks this as ‘itu um atu’, the same situation as 1141, the hero speaking to the tōḻi. Arumai (அருமை) here means ‘difficulty of attainment’, which he explains as caused by failed trysts (alla kuṟi) and obstacles (iṭaiyīṭu); the town, unaware of it, has made her seem ‘easy’ (eḷiyaḷ) and so has ‘given’ (īntatu) him the rumour, a word chosen because the rumour is his support. Malar aṉṉa kaṇṇāḷ, ‘she whose eyes are like flowers’ (Puliyur Kesikan specifies the kuvaḷai or blue water-lily), is a conventional epithet. Manakkudavar reads arumai as the nobility of her birth (iṟpiṟappu), so that the gossips speak of her as of a common girl. The text agrees on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com.

tamil:
உறாஅதோ ஊரறிந்த கௌவை அதனைப்
பெறாஅது பெற்றன்ன நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
uRaaadhoa ooraRindha keLavai adhanaip
peRaaadhu petranna neerththu
current_meaning: Is not the rumour the whole town knows a gain for me? Hearing it, my heart feels as if it already has the union it has not yet won.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever wanted a puppy so much that, when your friends started saying, ‘You’re getting a puppy!’, you felt almost as happy as if it were already sitting in your lap? The young man in this verse feels that way. The town’s talk about him and his beloved makes him feel as if they were already together.
university_explanation: Again ‘itu um atu’ in Parimelazhagar: the hero speaks. Uṟāatō (உறாஅதோ, with the alapeṭai lengthening) is a rhetorical question, ‘does it not come to me?’, and kauvai (கௌவை) is a synonym of alar; peṟāatu peṟṟaṉṉa nīrttu means ‘it has the nature of having got what was not got’. Parimelazhagar supplies maṉam, ‘my mind’, as the subject of nīrttu and glosses the phrase as having a joy like that of actual union. Manakkudavar reads it as the hero telling the tōḻi that the rumour should be welcomed, since through it the family will come to consent. The sources print கெளவை, which is a common encoding of கௌவை (kau) with separate vowel signs; this edition normalises it to கௌவை, as thirukkural.com’s Parimelazhagar text has it.

tamil:
கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம் அதுவின்றேல்
தவ்வென்னும் தன்மை இழந்து.
transliteration:
kavvaiyaal kavvidhu kaamam adhuvindrael
thavvennum thanmai izhandhu
current_meaning: My love grows and blooms on the town’s gossip; without that gossip it would lose its nature and shrink away.
elementary_explanation: Think of a small campfire. If nobody adds sticks, it gets smaller and goes out. The town’s chatter is like sticks thrown on this young man’s love: every time people talk, his love burns brighter. Without the talk, he says, it would shrink like a fire nobody feeds.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar again treats this as the hero’s speech. He explains the pun kavvaiyāl kavvitu: just as one says cevvitu of what has cevvai, the poet coins kavvitu, ‘full of kavvai’, and he glosses it as ‘has blossomed’ (alartal), with a play on alar, ‘rumour’, and alar, ‘to blossom’; the line means love ‘blossoms more and more’ on the rumour. Tavveṉṉum is an onomatopoeic expression (kuṟippu moḻi) for shrinking, which he supports with Neṭunalvāṭai 184-85. Its ‘nature’ (iyalpu) he defines as giving joy. Kavvai here is a variant form of kauvai, used for the pun; all three sources print the same text.

tamil:
களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால் காமம்
வெளிப்படுந் தோறும் இனிது.
transliteration:
kaLiththoRum kaLLuNdal vaettatraal kaamam
veLippatunh thoaRum inidhu
current_meaning: Just as a drinker wants more toddy each time it makes him merry, my love grows sweeter each time it is made public by the rumour.
elementary_explanation: Some sweets are so tasty that each one makes you want another. The young man says his love is like that. Each time people talk about it, it feels sweeter, and he wants it talked about even more.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar again gives this to the hero and explains vēṭṭaṟṟāl as a shortened form of vēṭkappaṭṭaṟṟāl, ‘as it is desired’: for drinkers, drinking toddy (kaḷ) grows sweeter each time they become merry (kaḷittoṟum), and so the hero’s love grows sweeter each time it is made known (veḷippaṭuntoṟum) by rumour. His point is that the very strength of desire makes even scandal pleasant. Manakkudavar assigns the couplet differently, to the tōḻi answering a hero who asked whether the rumour distressed them. The simile is striking given that chapter 93, kaḷḷuṇṇāmai, condemns drink; here the image describes the lover’s state without endorsing drinking. The text agrees in all three sources.

tamil:
கண்டது மன்னும் ஒருநாள் அலர்மன்னும்
திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண் டற்று.
transliteration:
kaNdadhu mannum orunhaaL alarmannum
thingaLaip paampukoN tatru
current_meaning: I saw my beloved only once, yet the rumour of it has spread everywhere, like the news when the serpent swallows the moon.
elementary_explanation: When there is an eclipse and the moon goes dark, everybody in the whole town talks about it at once. The girl in this verse says she met her sweetheart just one single time, and now the whole town is talking about them, as if it were an eclipse!
university_explanation: Here the speaker changes. Parimelazhagar says the heroine, kept from the hero by obstacles and failed trysts, speaks to the tōḻi while the hero is within earshot (ciṟaippuṟam), announcing the rumour to press him to marry. Kaṇṭatu ‘what I saw’ took place ‘on one day’ (orunāḷ), but the alar is ‘like the serpent seizing the moon’ (tiṅkaḷaip pāmpu koṇṭaṟṟu), the eclipse caused by Rāhu that everyone sees and talks about; Parimelazhagar notes that the effect (the universal talk) is described by naming the cause, and that both maṉṉum and the um are expletives (acai nilai). His moral is that a love that draws rumour even without meetings cannot go on, and must end in marriage. Kalaignar glosses the image explicitly as the eclipse (kirakaṇam).

tamil:
ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல்
நீராக நீளும்இந் நோய்.
transliteration:
ooravar kavai eruvaaka annaisol
neeraaka neeLum-inh noai
current_meaning: This lovesickness grows like a crop, with the town’s gossip as its manure and my mother’s angry words as its water.
elementary_explanation: A farmer puts manure on a plant and waters it, and the plant grows tall. The girl in this verse says the town’s gossip is like manure for her love, and her mother’s scolding is like water. Instead of stopping her love, they make it grow bigger and bigger.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar sets this in a later situation: the marriage is delayed, the heroine is suffering, and the tōḻi, knowing the hero is within earshot, tells her to bear up in view of the town’s talk and her mother’s words; this is her reply. Nōy (நோய்), ‘illness’, is the love-sickness, imagined as a crop (payir) through a partial metaphor (ēkatēca uruvakam): ūravar kauvai, the talk of the town’s women (he notes ūravar here excludes men, by what they do), is eru (எரு), ‘manure’, and aṉṉai col, the mother’s angry words (veñcol), is nīr, ‘water’, so it nīḷum, ‘keeps growing’. His comment is that the very things that should have made it shrink make it spread, and the intended effect is that the hero will marry. The sources print கெளவை for kauvai and the sandhi-joined நீளும்இந்; the reading is otherwise unvaried.

tamil:
நெய்யால் எரிநுதுப்பேம் என்றற்றால் கௌவையால்
காமம் நுதுப்பேம் எனல்.
transliteration:
neyyaal erinhudhuppaem endratraal kavvaiyaal
Kaamam nudhuppeam enal
current_meaning: To think that gossip can put out love is like thinking you can put out a fire by pouring ghee on it.
elementary_explanation: If you pour water on a fire, it goes out. But if you pour oil or butter on it, it flares up even higher! The girl in this verse says people who try to stop love by gossiping are making the same mistake: they are pouring butter on the fire.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar marks this ‘itu um atu’, continuing the heroine’s speech of 1147. Nutuppēm (நுதுப்பேம்) means ‘we shall extinguish’; ney (நெய்), ‘ghee, clarified butter’, is the classic accelerant of the sacrificial fire. He notes that the third-case endings (-āl) are instrumental and sums up: love cannot be extinguished by rumour, which is the very cause of its flaring up. Manakkudavar assigns the couplet to the tōḻi, speaking when the hero still wants to continue the secret affair. The comparison of desire to fire fed with ghee is widespread in Indian literature, notably in Manu and in the story of Yayati, which gives this couplet unusually direct parallels. The text agrees in all three sources apart from the கெளவை spelling, normalised here.

tamil:
அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ அஞ்சலோம்பு என்றார்
பலர்நாண நீத்தக் கடை.
transliteration:
alarnhaaNa olvadhoa anjaloambu endraar
palarnhaaNa neeththak kadai
current_meaning: He once told me, ‘Do not be afraid,’ and now he has left me in a way that shames me before many; how can I still be ashamed of the town’s gossip?
elementary_explanation: Imagine a friend promised, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll always stay with you,’ and then went away, so everyone could see you were left alone. You might think, ‘Everyone already knows I’ve been left. Why should I be embarrassed about what they say now?’ That is how the girl in this verse feels.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar sets this when the hero has gone away, leaving the marriage still pending; the heroine, aware he has returned and is within earshot, answers the tōḻi who told her to endure for fear of the rumour. Añcal ōmpu (அஞ்சல் ஓம்பு), ‘guard against fear, do not fear’, recalls the hero’s promise at their first meeting, ‘I will not leave you’; now he has abandoned her ‘so that the many are ashamed’ (palar nāṇa), and she asks whether she can still feel nāṇ before alar. He paraphrases her meaning: ‘We, who are in a state that makes onlookers blush, where is our shame?’ Manakkudavar takes the ‘many’ as the tōḻi, the foster-mother (cevili) and the household. Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss reads the line differently, as the hero having said ‘fear not’ even as he departed; the text itself agrees in all three sources.

tamil:
தாம்வேண்டின் நல்குவர் காதலர் யாம்வேண்டும்
கௌவை எடுக்கும்இவ் வூர்.
transliteration:
thaamvaeNtin nalkuvar kaadhalar yaamvaendum
kavvai edukkum-iv voor
current_meaning: The town is now raising just the rumour we wanted; so if we ask him, our lover will gladly agree to what we want.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you have been hoping your parents will let you go on a trip with your best friend. Then everybody starts saying, ‘Those two always go everywhere together!’ The talk makes the trip seem natural, and you feel sure your friend will say yes when you ask. That is how the girl’s friend feels in this verse.
university_explanation: In Parimelazhagar’s reading the speaker is now the tōḻi, addressing the heroine while the hero is within earshot, to make him favour elopement (uṭaṉpōkku). ‘The rumour we have long wanted’ (yām vēṇṭum kauvai), wanted because it gives a reason for leaving together, ‘the town itself is raising’ (eṭukkum); kātalar, ‘the lover’, chosen to suggest that because he loves her he will not refuse, ‘will grant it if we ask’ (tām vēṇṭiṉ nalkuvar). He closes his commentary by noting that the twenty couplets of chapters 114 and 115 are all puṇartal nimittam, occasions leading toward union. Manakkudavar reads the second clause differently, that the family will now themselves agree to give her to the lover; modern glosses (Pappaiah: he will marry me; Varadarasanar: he will grant it) vary between marriage and elopement.

tamil:
செல்லாமை உண்டேல் எனக்குரை மற்றுநின்
வல்வரவு வாழ்வார்க் குரை.
transliteration:
Sellaamai undael enakkurai matrunin
valvaravu vaazhvaark kurai.
current_meaning: If you are not going to leave, tell me so; but if your news is that you will go and hurry back, tell it to whoever will still be alive when you return.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your best friend says, ‘I’m moving away, but don’t worry, I’ll visit soon!’ You might answer, ‘Only tell me the part where you’re staying. The coming-back-soon part is too far away for me to hold on to.’ The wife in this couplet feels the same: a promise to return quickly is no comfort if her heart cannot last that long.
university_explanation: Chapter 116 opens the karpiyal (the section on married love) with the heroine’s distress when her husband announces a journey, conventionally to earn wealth or serve the king; commentators assign the couplets to the heroine herself or to her confidante (tōḻi) speaking for her. Cellāmai (செல்லாமை) is ‘not going’, and valvaravu (வல்வரவு) is ‘swift return’; the sting is in vāḻvārkku urai, ‘tell it to those who will live’, implying that she will not survive the interval. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘tell it to those able to stay alive until then’, while Kalaignar turns it into ‘say your farewells now to whoever will still be alive when you come back’. Pope renders: ‘If you will say, “I leave thee not,” then tell me so; / Of quick return tell those that can survive this woe.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்கண் உடைத்தவர் பார்வல் பிரிவஞ்சும்
புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு.
transliteration:
Inkan udaiththavar paarval pirivanjum
punkan udaiththaal punarvu.
current_meaning: Once, even his look was pure delight; now even our embrace is filled with pain, because I dread the parting that is coming.
elementary_explanation: Think of the last day of a wonderful holiday. You are still at the beach, the sun is shining, but you keep thinking, ‘Tomorrow we go home,’ and the fun feels a little sad. The wife in this couplet feels that way: her husband is still with her, but knowing he will leave makes even being close to him hurt.
university_explanation: The couplet contrasts the past and present of the same relationship: avar pārval (அவர் பார்வல், ‘his look’) once had iṉkaṇ (இன்கண், ‘sweetness, joy’), but now even puṇarvu (புணர்வு, ‘union, being together’) has puṉkaṇ (புன்கண், ‘distress’) because of pirivu añcum, ‘fearing separation’. The two rhyming nouns iṉkaṇ and puṉkaṇ carry the turn from joy to grief. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read pārval as his loving look, while Solomon Pappaiah contrasts his pleasing look with his conduct, which signals that he is about to leave; Kalaignar sharpens the contrast between gazing and embracing. Pope: ‘It once was perfect joy to look upon his face; / But now the fear of parting saddens each embrace.’

tamil:
அரிதரோ தேற்றம் அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்
பிரிவோ ரிடத்துண்மை யான்.
transliteration:
Aridharo thaetram arivudaiyaar kannum
pirivo ritaththunmai yaan.
current_meaning: Since parting happens at some time even with a wise and understanding lover, it is hard to feel sure of anyone’s promise never to leave.
elementary_explanation: Suppose the kindest, smartest grown-up you know promises, ‘I’ll always be here.’ Then one day they have to go away for work. Next time someone promises you that, it is harder to believe, even if they mean it. The wife in this couplet feels the same: if even a wise, loving husband sometimes leaves, how can she trust any promise to stay?
university_explanation: Tēṟṟam (தேற்றம்) means ‘certainty, confidence’ and arito (அரிதரோ, with the emphatic particle aro) ‘is indeed hard’. Aṟivuṭaiyār kaṇṇum (அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்), ‘even in those who have understanding’, refers to the husband, who knows how much his absence will hurt; pirivu ōr iṭattu uṇmaiyāṉ (பிரிவு ஓர் இடத்து உண்மையான்), ‘since separation exists at one time or another’, gives the reason. The printed form pirivō riṭattuṇmai is a sandhi run-together of pirivu ōr iṭattu uṇmai, and editions agree on the wording. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take tēṟṟam to be her confidence in his ‘I will not leave’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as her inability to be sure of his love. Pope: ‘To trust henceforth is hard, if ever he depart, / E’en he, who knows his promise and my breaking heart.’

tamil:
அளித்தஞ்சல் என்றவர் நீப்பின் தெளித்தசொல்
தேறியார்க்கு உண்டோ தவறு.
transliteration:
Aliththanjal endravar neeppin theliththasol
thaeriyaarkku undo thavaru.
current_meaning: If the one who lovingly said ‘Do not be afraid’ goes away, is it the fault of the one who believed his reassuring words?
elementary_explanation: Imagine a parent says, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll be right here,’ and then leaves the room. Would it be your fault for believing them? Of course not. The wife in this couplet asks the same question: her husband promised she need not fear, so how can she be blamed for trusting him?
university_explanation: Aḷittu (அளித்து) is ‘having shown grace, having loved’ and añcal (அஞ்சல்) is the prohibitive ‘do not fear’; together they recall the husband’s reassurance at the start of their life together, which Solomon Pappaiah places at the time of marriage. Nīppiṉ (நீப்பின்) is ‘if he leaves’, and teḷitta col tēṟiyārkku (தெளித்த சொல் தேறியார்க்கு) ‘to those who trusted the words that made them clear (free of doubt)’. The question uṇṭō tavaṟu (உண்டோ தவறு, ‘is there any fault?’) is rhetorical: the fault lies with the one who promised. Commentators agree on this reading; Pope: ‘If he depart, who fondly said, “Fear not,” what blame’s incurred / By those who trusted to his reassuring word?’

tamil:
ஓம்பின் அமைந்தார் பிரிவோம்பல் மற்றவர்
நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு.
transliteration:
Ompin amaindhaar pirivompal matravar
neengin aridhaal punarvu.
current_meaning: If you want to save me, keep my husband from going; for once he has left, being together again will be hard to come by.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever seen a balloon start to float away? It is much easier to hold the string tight before it leaves your hand than to catch the balloon once it is in the sky. The wife in this couplet says the same: stop him from leaving now, because once he is gone, getting him back will be very hard.
university_explanation: Ompiṉ (ஓம்பின்) is ‘if you would protect (me)’, and amaintār (அமைந்தார்) ‘the one who is fitted (to me)’, that is, her destined husband; pirivu ōmpal (பிரிவு ஓம்பல்) means ‘prevent the parting’. The warning follows: avar nīṅkiṉ arito puṇarvu (அவர் நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு), ‘if he leaves, union is hard’, with the commentarial suggestion that she may not live to see his return. Commentators take the couplet as the heroine’s words to her confidante, asking her to stop the departure; Solomon Pappaiah instead has the husband himself, as the one whose role is to protect her life, avoid leaving her. Pope: ‘If you would guard my life, from going him restrain / Who fills my life! If he depart, hardly we meet again.’

tamil:
பிரிவுரைக்கும் வன்கண்ணர் ஆயின் அரிதவர்
நல்குவர் என்னும் நசை.
transliteration:
Pirivuraikkum vankannar aayin aridhavar
nalkuvar ennum nasai.
current_meaning: If he is hard-hearted enough to tell me to my face that he is leaving, then my hope that he will come back and be kind to me is a hope I can hardly keep.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a friend who can say ‘I’m going, bye!’ without looking sad at all. You might think, ‘If leaving me is that easy for them, will they really hurry back?’ The wife in this couplet thinks the same about her husband.
university_explanation: Pirivu uraikkum (பிரிவு உரைக்கும்) is ‘who speaks of parting’ and vaṉkaṇṇar (வன்கண்ணர்) ‘the hard-eyed, the cruel’: the very fact that he can announce the separation shows a hardness she did not expect. Nalkuvar (நல்குவர்) is ‘he will show grace or love’ and nacai (நசை) ‘longing hope’, which is arito, ‘hard to hold’ or, as most commentators read it, futile. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses vaṉkaṇ as ‘a heart of stone’ and Kalaignar calls the hope ‘vain’; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the parting is for work. Pope: ‘To cherish longing hope that he should ever gracious be, / Is hard, when he could stand, and of departure speak to me.’

tamil:
துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல் முன்கை
இறைஇறவா நின்ற வளை.
transliteration:
Thuraivan thurandhamai thootraakol munkai
iraiiravaa nindra valai.
current_meaning: The bangles slipping down past the joint of my forearm, now that I have grown thin, will surely announce to the whole town that the lord of the seashore has left me.
elementary_explanation: When you are very sad, people can often tell even if you say nothing: your face looks different and you don’t feel like eating. In this couplet the wife has grown so thin with sadness that her bangles slide down her arm, and everyone who sees them knows her husband has gone away.
university_explanation: Tuṟaivaṉ (துறைவன்) is ‘lord of the shore’, the hero of the neytal (seashore) landscape, and tuṟantamai (துறந்தமை) ‘his having left’; tūṟṟākol (தூற்றாகொல்) asks ‘will they not proclaim (it abroad)?’, from tūṟṟu, ‘to spread gossip, publicise’. Muṉkai iṟai iṟavā niṉṟa vaḷai (முன்கை இறை இறவா நின்ற வளை) describes bangles ‘passing beyond the wrist-joint of the forearm’ because her arm has wasted, the standard Sangam sign of a woman pining in separation. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Kalaignar) read the bangles as announcing his departure to the town; Solomon Pappaiah reads them as telling the heroine herself that he plans to leave, and Pope’s ‘announced before’ follows that anticipatory sense. Pope: ‘The bracelet slipping from my wrist announced before / Departure of the Prince that rules the ocean shore.’

tamil:
இன்னாது இனன்இல்ஊர் வாழ்தல் அதனினும்
இன்னாது இனியார்ப் பிரிவு.
transliteration:
Innaadhu inanil oor vaazhdhal adhaninum
innaadhu iniyaarp pirivu.
current_meaning: It is painful to live in a town where no one is close to you; it is more painful still to be parted from the one you love.
elementary_explanation: Being the new kid in a school where you don’t know anyone feels lonely. But being far away from the person you love most feels even lonelier, even if you are surrounded by people. That is what this couplet says.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a graded comparison: iṉṉātu (இன்னாது, ‘painful’) is repeated, first for living in an iṉaṉ il ūr (இனன் இல் ஊர்), ‘a town without one’s own kind or kin’, and then, with ataṉiṉum (அதனினும், ‘more than that’), for iṉiyār pirivu (இனியார்ப் பிரிவு), ‘separation from the sweet one’. Iṉam can mean kin, friends of one’s own sort, or (for the heroine) companions such as the confidante, which Puliyur Kesikan specifies; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘those who love us as our own’. The repetition of iṉṉātu echoes the device of the Iṉṉā Nāṟpatu, a didactic work among the Eighteen Minor Classics. Pope: ‘’Tis sad to sojourn in the town where no kind kinsmen dwell; / ’Tis sadder still to bid a friend beloved farewell.’

tamil:
தொடிற்சுடின் அல்லது காமநோய் போல
விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ.
transliteration:
Thotirsudin alladhu kaamanoi pola
vitirsudal aatrumo thee.
current_meaning: Fire burns only when you touch it; can fire, like the sickness of love, burn you even when you move away from it?
elementary_explanation: A campfire only hurts if you touch it; step back and you are safe. But missing someone you love is a strange kind of fire: it hurts more the farther away they are. This couplet points out how odd and how painful that is.
university_explanation: The couplet is a vētṟumai (contrast) built on fire: toṭiṉ cuṭiṉ allatu (தொடின் சுடின் அல்லது), ‘other than burning when touched’, set against viṭiṉ cuṭal (விடின் சுடல்), ‘burning when let go of, when apart’. Kāmanōy (காமநோய்), ‘love-sickness’, is the subject that has this power, and āṟṟumō (ஆற்றுமோ), ‘is it able?’, makes it a rhetorical question to which the answer is no. Commentators agree on the reading; Kalaignar expands it to the lovers neither seeing nor touching each other, and Solomon Pappaiah renders it simply. The image is one of the most quoted in the Kāmattuppāl. Pope: ‘Fire burns the hands that touch; but smart of love / Will burn in hearts that far away remove.’

tamil:
அரிதாற்றி அல்லல்நோய் நீக்கிப் பிரிவாற்றிப்
பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்.
transliteration:
Aridhaatri allalnoi neekkip pirivaatrip
pinirundhu vaazhvaar palar.
current_meaning: Many people, it seems, can agree to what should be impossible, drive away the pain of it, bear the separation, and still go on living afterwards.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes a grown-up says, ‘Lots of people manage when someone they love goes away,’ and you think, ‘Maybe they do, but I don’t know how I would!’ The wife in this couplet says something like that: other people may be able to bear it, but she is not sure she can.
university_explanation: The couplet strings together four participles: aritu āṟṟi (அரிது ஆற்றி), ‘bearing what is hard’ or consenting to the impossible; allal nōy nīkki (அல்லல் நோய் நீக்கி), ‘driving off the sickness of sorrow’; pirivu āṟṟi (பிரிவு ஆற்றி), ‘enduring the separation’; and piṉ iruntu vāḻvār (பின் இருந்து வாழ்வார்), ‘those who live on afterwards’, before the predicate palar (பலர்), ‘are many’. Commentators differ on the tone: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as a straightforward observation that many women endure, Solomon Pappaiah as a statement about wives whose husbands go to earn, while Kalaignar and Pope’s prose gloss (‘As if there were many indeed…’) take it as irony, so that the heroine implies she is not one of them. The chapter title, Pirivāṟṟāmai, ‘not being able to bear separation’, supports the ironic reading. Pope’s verse: ‘Sorrow’s sadness meek sustaining, Driving sore distress away, / Separation uncomplaining Many bear the livelong day!’

tamil:
மறைப்பேன்மன் யானிஃதோ நோயை இறைப்பவர்க்கு
ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்.
transliteration:
Maraippaenman yaaniqdhoa noayai iraippavarkku
ootruneer poala mikum.
current_meaning: I would hide this pain of love from others, but like the water of a spring that rises the more it is drawn, it only swells the more I try to hide it.
elementary_explanation: Think of a well in a garden: every bucket you pull out, the spring at the bottom fills it up again, even higher. The wife in this verse misses her husband, and she tries to keep her sadness a secret, but every time she pushes it down, it bubbles back up, bigger than before.
university_explanation: Chapter 117 belongs to the karpiyal (married love) and follows the husband’s departure in Chapter 116; its title joins padar (படர், the anguish of longing), melindhu (மெலிந்து, growing thin) and irangal (இரங்கல், lamenting), and commentators read most of its couplets as the heroine’s replies to her confidante (tōḻi), who urges her to bear the separation quietly. The image turns on iṟaippavarkku (இறைப்பவர்க்கு, ‘for those who bail or draw water’) and ūṟṟunīr (ஊற்றுநீர், spring water): concealment works like drawing from a spring, which only makes it flow faster. Man (மன்) is a particle of unrealised wish, ‘I would indeed hide it, but…’, and nōy (நோய், ‘sickness’) is the standard Kural word for love-pain. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss ‘the more I hide it, the more it grows’, and Pope renders: ‘I would my pain conceal, but see! it surging swells, / As streams to those that draw from ever-springing wells.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கரத்தலும் ஆற்றேன்இந் நோயைநோய் செய்தார்க்கு
உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Karaththalum aatraeninh noayainoai seydhaarkku
uraiththalum naanuth tharum.
current_meaning: I cannot keep this love-pain hidden, and yet to tell it to the one who caused it fills me with shame.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you miss someone so much that everyone can see it on your face, but when you think of phoning them to say ‘I miss you’, you feel too shy. You are stuck in the middle: you cannot hide it and you cannot say it. That is exactly how the wife in this verse feels.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two failures side by side with the double -um (‘both… and’): karattal (கரத்தல், concealing) is beyond her strength (āṟṟēṉ, ஆற்றேன், ‘I am unable’), and uraittal (உரைத்தல், telling) brings nāṇ (நாண், modesty, shame). The phrase nōy ceytārkku (நோய் செய்தார்க்கு, ‘to the one who caused the sickness’) is pointed: the cure and the cause are the same person. Puliyur Kesikan reads the telling as sending a message (tūtu) to the absent husband, which modesty forbids, while Solomon Pappaiah modernises it to writing or telephoning. Nāṇ is one of the defining virtues of the Tamil heroine, and the Kamattuppal repeatedly stages its struggle with kāmam (desire), most fully in Chapter 114 and in the next couplet. Pope: ‘I cannot hide this pain of mine, yet shame restrains / When I would tell it out to him who caused my pains.’ The words are identical on both base sources, with only a spacing difference at ஆற்றேன்இந்.

tamil:
காமமும் நாணும் உயிர்காவாத் தூங்கும்என்
நோனா உடம்பின் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Kaamamum naanum uyirkaavaath thoongumen
noanaa udampin akaththu.
current_meaning: Within my body, which can no longer bear it, love and shame hang from either end of a carrying pole, and my very life is that pole.
elementary_explanation: Have you seen someone carry two heavy buckets on a stick across their shoulders? The wife says her heart is like that stick: on one side hangs her love for her husband, on the other her shyness, and both are so heavy she feels she might break.
university_explanation: The central image is the kāvu (காவு) or kāvaḍi, a shoulder pole with loads at each end: uyir (உயிர், life) is the pole, and kāmam (காமம், desire) and nāṇ (நாண், modesty) hang (tūṅgum, தூங்கும்) in balance from it. Nōṉā uṭampu (நோனா உடம்பு) is ‘the body that cannot endure’, already worn thin by separation, which carries the whole apparatus. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah spell out the two loads exactly as love-pain and the shame of not being able to tell it, linking this couplet to 1162; Kalaignar describes the suffering body itself as a kāvaḍi. The image is admired in the commentary tradition because the balance is the torment: neither load can be dropped without the other swinging. Pope: ‘My soul, like porter’s pole, within my wearied frame, / Sustains a two-fold burthen poised, of love and shame.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

tamil:
காமக் கடல்மன்னும் உண்டே அதுநீந்தும்
ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்.
transliteration:
Kaamak kadalmannum undae adhuneendhum
aemap punaimannum il.
current_meaning: There is indeed a sea of love before me, but there is no safe raft on which to cross it.
elementary_explanation: Picture standing on a beach looking at a huge ocean you need to cross, but there is no boat, not even a little raft. That is how the wife feels about her love while her husband is away: it is as big as the sea, and the one who could carry her across is not here.
university_explanation: The couplet balances two clauses with the emphatic particle maṉṉum (மன்னும், ‘indeed’): there is (uṇṭē) a sea of kāmam, and there is no (il) ēmap puṇai (ஏமப் புணை), a ‘raft of safety’. Puṇai (புணை) is a float or raft, and ēmam (ஏமம்) means protection or security. Puliyur Kesikan identifies the missing raft as the husband himself, who alone could carry her across and is now absent, while Solomon Pappaiah reads the sea as love-pain that has outgrown the shame of the previous couplet. The sea image recurs at 1166 and 1167, and readers have long noted its echo of the Kural’s opening chapter (Kural 10), where the ‘great sea of births’ is crossed only by those who cling to the feet of God: here the ocean is love and no such crossing is available. Pope: ‘A sea of love, ’tis true, I see stretched out before, / But not the trusty bark that wafts to yonder shore.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

tamil:
துப்பின் எவனாவர் மன்கொல் துயர்வரவு
நட்பினுள் ஆற்று பவர்.
transliteration:
Thuppin evanaavar mankol thuyarvaravu
natpinul aatru pavar.
current_meaning: If he can bring me such sorrow while we are lovers, what would he do to me if he were my enemy?
elementary_explanation: Imagine your best friend forgets your birthday and it really hurts. You might say, ‘If this is how much my friend can hurt me, I would hate to see what an enemy could do!’ The wife is half-joking, half-hurt in the same way about her husband who has gone away.
university_explanation: The couplet is ironic reproach: the husband ‘accomplishes the coming of sorrow’ (tuyar varavu āṟṟupavar, துயர்வரவு ஆற்றுபவர்) even within naṭpu (நட்பு, friendship, intimacy), so what (evaṉ, எவன்) would he become in tuppu (துப்பு)? The commentators divide over tuppu: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take it as ‘strength’, the power needed against a foe, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take it directly as ‘enmity’ (pakai), and the sense is the same either way. Maṉ kol (மன்கொல்) adds wondering doubt. The reproach is affectionate rather than bitter, in keeping with the karpu ideal in which the wife complains of, but does not renounce, the absent husband. Pope: ‘Who work us woe in friendship’s trustful hour, / What will they prove when angry tempests lower?’ The text is identical on both base sources.

tamil:
இன்பம் கடல்மற்றுக் காமம் அஃதடுங்கால்
துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது.
transliteration:
Inpam kadalmatruk kaamam aqdhadungaal
thunpam adhanir peridhu.
current_meaning: The joy of love is as vast as the sea, but when love turns to torment, its sorrow is even greater than the sea.
elementary_explanation: When your best friend is with you, the fun feels as big as the ocean. But when they move far away, the missing-them feeling can seem even bigger than that ocean. The wife says love works like that: the happy part is huge, and the sad part is huger still.
university_explanation: The couplet sets inpam (இன்பம், joy) against tunpam (துன்பம், sorrow) with kaṭal (கடல், sea) as the unit of measure: love’s joy is a sea, and its pain, when it aṭuṅkāl (அடுங்கால், ‘when it torments’), is periṭu (பெரிது), greater than that. Maṟṟu (மற்று) marks the turn, ‘but then’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take the contrast as union versus separation, which fits the chapter’s setting. The sea of 1164 thus grows: there it was a sea without a raft, here the sorrow exceeds the sea. Pope: ‘A happy love’s sea of joy; but mightier sorrows roll / From unpropitious love athwart the troubled soul.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

tamil:
காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்திக் கரைகாணேன்
யாமத்தும் யானே உளேன்.
transliteration:
Kaamak kadumpunal neendhik karaikaanaen
yaamaththum yaanae ulaen.
current_meaning: I swim the fierce flood of love but see no shore; even in the middle of the night, I alone am awake.
