elementary_explanation: Imagine swimming and swimming in a huge lake at night, looking for the edge, and never finding it, while everyone else is fast asleep in bed. That is how the wife feels: her missing-him feeling seems to have no end, and at midnight she is the only one still awake.
university_explanation: Kaṭum puṉal (கடும்புனல்) is a ‘fierce flood’ or torrent, extending the sea of 1164 and 1166 into a current she must swim; karai kāṇēṉ (கரைகாணேன்) is ‘I see no shore’. Yāmam (யாமம்) is the midnight watch, and yāṉē uḷēṉ (யானே உளேன்), ‘I alone am’, is read by all four modern glossators as ‘I alone remain awake’, while Pope’s commentary-based prose adds ‘still I live’, catching the other shade of uḷēṉ (‘I exist, I survive’). The couplet introduces the night theme that the next two couplets develop. Pope’s verse: ‘I swim the cruel tide of love, and can no shore descry, / In watches of the night, too, ’mid the waters, only I!’ The text is identical on both base sources.

tamil:
மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி அளித்திரா
என்னல்லது இல்லை துணை.
transliteration:
Mannuyir ellaam thuyitri aliththiraa
ennalladhu illai thunai.
current_meaning: Poor night! It has lulled every living thing to sleep, and now it has no companion but me.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever been the only one awake in the house at night? Everyone is asleep, it is very quiet, and you feel like it is just you and the dark. The wife feels so lonely that she starts feeling sorry for the night itself, because the only friend the night has left is her.
university_explanation: The couplet personifies irā (இரா, night): it has put to sleep (tuyiṟṟi, துயிற்றி) all ‘abiding lives’ (maṉṉuyir, மன்னுயிர்), and now has no tuṇai (துணை, companion) except (allatu) me. Aḷittu (அளித்து) is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as ‘pitiable’ (‘this night is to be pitied’), while Pope’s commentary-based prose takes it as ‘graciously’ (‘the night which graciously lulls to sleep all living creatures’). The irony is turned inward: by pitying the night’s solitude the heroine reveals her own. Kalaignar makes it an address, ‘O Night!’. Pope’s verse: ‘All living souls in slumber soft she steeps; / But me alone kind night for her companing keeps!’ The text is identical on both base sources.

tamil:
கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள்
நெடிய கழியும் இரா.
transliteration:
Kotiyaar kodumaiyin thaamkotiya innaal
netiya kazhiyum iraa.
current_meaning: These nights that drag on so long are crueller even than the cruelty of the cruel one who left me.
elementary_explanation: When you are waiting for something you really want, like a birthday, the days feel super long. The wife waiting for her husband says the long nights are even meaner to her than her husband was for going away.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on koṭu (கொடு, cruel): koṭiyār (கொடியார், ‘the cruel one’, the departed husband), koṭumai (கொடுமை, cruelty) and koṭiya (கொடிய, cruel) are stacked so that the nights, iṉṉāḷ neṭiya kaḻiyum irā (‘the nights which in these days pass so long’), outdo the husband in cruelty. The comparison lets the heroine blame the nights rather than the husband, softening the reproach of 1165. There is a sandhi variant in the first line: ytamizh.com prints தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள், while thirukkural.net prints தாம்கொடிய விந்நாள், with the glide v of koṭiya + iṉṉāḷ written out; the reading is the same. Pope: ‘More cruel than the cruelty of him, the cruel one, / In these sad times are lengthening hours of night I watch alone.’

tamil:
உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின் வெள்ளநீர்
நீந்தல மன்னோஎன் கண்.
transliteration:
Ullampoandru ulvazhich chelkirpin vellaneer
neendhala mannoaen kan.
current_meaning: If my eyes could travel like my heart to where he is, they would not have to swim in this flood of tears.
elementary_explanation: Your thoughts can fly anywhere: you can imagine being with your grandma far away in a second. But your eyes cannot go there to see her. The wife says her heart is already with her husband, but her eyes are stuck at home, so they just cry and cry.
university_explanation: The closing couplet contrasts uḷḷam (உள்ளம், heart or mind), which goes freely to uḷvaḻi (உள்வழி, ‘the place where he is’), with kaṇ (கண், the eyes), which cannot follow and so must ‘swim’ (nīntu, நீந்து) in veḷḷa nīr (வெள்ளநீர், a flood of water), that is, tears. Celkiṟpiṉ (செல்கிற்பின்) is ‘if they were able to go’, and maṉṉō (மன்னோ) adds regretful emphasis. Puliyur Kesikan extends the wish to her whole body going where her heart is, while the other glossators keep to the eyes. The flood of this couplet answers the floods of 1164 and 1167: the sea of love has become the water of her own tears, and the next chapter (118, kaṇ vitumpu aḻital) turns entirely to the eyes. Pope: ‘When eye of mine would as my soul go forth to him, / It knows not how through floods of its own tears to swim.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

tamil:
கண்தாம் கலுழ்வ தெவன்கொலோ தண்டாநோய்
தாம்காட்ட யாம்கண் டது.
transliteration:
Kandhaam kaluzhva thevan-koloa thandaanoi
thaamkaatta yaamkan dadhu.
current_meaning: This unending love-sickness came to me only because my eyes showed him to me; so why do those same eyes now weep and beg to see him?
elementary_explanation: Imagine you begged your friend to let you hold their puppy, and then you cried when it was time to give it back. Your friend might say, ‘But you were the one who wanted to hold it!’ The lady in this couplet scolds her own eyes the same way: they were the ones who looked at him first, so why are they crying now?
university_explanation: Chapter 118 continues the karpiyal (married love) sequence on separation, and its whole conceit is that the heroine turns on her own eyes: kaṇ (eye) plus vituppu (eager longing, impatience) plus aḻital (wasting away), i.e. the eyes are worn out by their own craving to see the absent husband. In the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar she speaks to her confidante (tōḻi), half-blaming, half-pitying the eyes as if they were separate persons. Kaluḻvatu (கலுழ்வது) is ‘weeping’, taṇṭā nōy (தண்டாநோய்) ‘the disease that does not abate’, and tām kāṭṭa yām kaṇṭatu ‘we saw it because they showed it’: the eyes are both cause and complainant. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen the irony by making the eyes weep to be shown him again, while Pope renders: ‘They showed me him, and then my endless pain / I saw: why then should weeping eyes complain?’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய உண்கண் பரிந்துணராப்
பைதல் உழப்பது எவன்.
transliteration:
Therindhunaraa noakkiya un-kan parindhunaraap
paidhal uzhappadhu evan.
current_meaning: My kohl-darkened eyes looked at him back then without weighing what would follow; why do they now suffer, without understanding that the sorrow is of their own making?
elementary_explanation: Think of someone who eats a whole bag of sweets without thinking, and then complains of a tummy ache as if it came from nowhere. The lady says her eyes did the same: they gazed at him without thinking ahead, and now they cry as if they don’t know why it hurts.
university_explanation: The couplet balances two negated verbs of knowing: terintu uṇarā nōkkiya, ‘looked without discerning and understanding’ (then), and parintu uṇarā, ‘not perceiving with sympathy’ or ‘not grasping’ (now). Uṇkaṇ (உண்கண்) is the conventional ‘eye fit to be eaten’, i.e. kohl-lined and lovely, and paital (பைதல்) is grief or affliction; uḻappatu evaṉ asks ‘why do they toil in it?’ Mu. Varadarasanar reads the second clause as the eyes failing to feel affection now; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as the eyes failing to recognise that they brought this on themselves and should bear it. Pope gives: ‘How glancing eyes, that rash unweeting looked that day, / With sorrow measureless are wasting now away!’ No textual variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கதுமெனத் தாநோக்கித் தாமே கலுழும்
இதுநகத் தக்க துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Kadhumenath thaanoakkith thaamae kaluzhum
ithunakath thakka thudaiththu.
current_meaning: These eyes rushed of their own accord to look at him, and now of their own accord they weep; surely that deserves to be laughed at.
elementary_explanation: Picture a child who runs to jump in a puddle, then cries because their socks are wet. It’s sad, but also a little funny, because they did it to themselves! The lady laughs at her eyes the same way: they hurried to look, and now they are the ones crying.
university_explanation: Katumeṉa (கதுமென) is an adverb of sudden speed, ‘in a flash’, and the parallel tām (themselves) / tāmē (they themselves) puts the whole action, the eager looking and the weeping, on the eyes alone. Naka-t-takkatu uṭaittu, ‘it has the quality of something to be laughed at’, gives the chapter its bitter humour: the heroine mocks her own organs. Puliyur Kesikan glosses the laughter as at the eyes’ ignorance; Solomon Pappaiah renders it colloquially, ‘when I see these eyes crying alone today, I can only laugh’. Pope: ‘The eyes that threw such eager glances round erewhile / Are weeping now. Such folly surely claims a smile!’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெயலாற்றா நீருலந்த உண்கண் உயலாற்றா
உய்வில்நோய் என்கண் நிறுத்து.
transliteration:
Peyalaatraa neerulandha un-kan uyalaatraa
uyvilnoi en-kan niruththu.
current_meaning: Having planted in me a disease I cannot escape or survive, my lovely eyes have wept until their tears are dried up and they can weep no more.
elementary_explanation: Imagine crying so hard and so long that, in the end, no more tears come out. That is how the lady’s eyes feel: they cried and cried, and now they are dry, but the sadness is still there.
university_explanation: Peyal (பெயல்) is literally ‘rain’, so peyal āṟṟā nīr ulanta is ‘the water dried up, no longer able to rain’: the tears themselves are exhausted. Uyal āṟṟā uyvil nōy is a doubled image of fatality, ‘a disease with no escape, which one cannot survive’, and eṉkaṇ niṟuttu ‘having fixed it in me’ (with a pun on kaṇ as both ‘eye’ and ‘in’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree that the eyes, having caused the incurable love-sickness, are now too dry even to weep. Pope: ‘Those eyes have wept till all the fount of tears is dry, / That brought upon me pain that knows no remedy.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
படலாற்றா பைதல் உழக்கும் கடலாற்றாக்
காமநோய் செய்தஎன் கண்.
transliteration:
Padalaatraa paidhal uzhakkum kadalaatraak
kaamanoi seydha-en kan.
current_meaning: My eyes, which brought on a love-sickness too great for even the sea to hold, now suffer the torment of being unable to sleep.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever been so worried about something that you couldn’t fall asleep, even though you were tired? The lady’s eyes feel that way every night. Her missing-him feeling is so big, bigger than the ocean, that her eyes just can’t close.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two ‘cannot’ compounds against each other: paṭal āṟṟā, ‘unable to lie down (sleep)’, and kaṭal āṟṟā, ‘which the sea cannot hold’, so that the eyes are punished by sleeplessness for a love-sickness larger than the ocean. Paital uḻakkum is ‘are tormented by affliction’. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the eyes suffer ‘through this evil deed’, at night, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar stress that the sickness was caused by the eyes and they now cannot sleep. Pope: ‘The eye that wrought me more than sea could hold of woes, / Is suffering pangs that banish all repose.’ No variant readings were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஓஒ இனிதே எமக்கிந்நோய் செய்தகண்
தாஅம் இதற்பட் டது.
transliteration:
Ohoh inidhae emakkinnoi seydhakan
thaa-am itharpat tadhu.
current_meaning: Oh, how sweet it is! The eyes that gave me this sickness have fallen into the same suffering themselves.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a friend talked you into jumping into a cold pool, and then they slipped and fell in too. You might shiver and giggle, ‘Ha! Now you know how it feels!’ The lady says that to her eyes: they got her into this sadness, and now they are stuck in it too.
university_explanation: The couplet opens with the long exclamation ōo (ஓஒ), an alapeṭai (prosodic lengthening) expressing intense feeling, and closes with the lengthened tāam (தாஅம், ‘they themselves’), both stretched for metre and emphasis. Iṉitē, ‘it is sweet’, is ironic satisfaction: the eyes that ‘made this sickness for us’ (emakku innōy ceyta kaṇ) have ‘fallen into it’ (itaṟpaṭṭatu). Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah specify that the eyes now cannot sleep and weep, while Kalaignar renders the tone as ‘this is a joy to me’. Pope: ‘Oho! how sweet a thing to see! the eye / That wrought this pain, in the same gulf doth lie.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உழந்துழந் துள்நீர் அறுக விழைந்திழைந்து
வேண்டி அவர்க்கண்ட கண்.
transliteration:
Uzhandhuzhan thulneer aruka vizhaindhizhaindhu
vaenti avarkkanda kan.
current_meaning: Let the eyes that once gazed on him with melting, eager longing now ache and ache until every tear within them is gone.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes when we feel very sad, we get a little cross with ourselves too. The lady is so sad that she tells her own eyes, ‘You wanted to look at him so much, so now you can cry until you have no tears left!’ It is her way of showing how much she misses him.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on two reduplicated verbs: uḻantu uḻantu, ‘suffering, suffering’, and viḻaintu iḻaintu, ‘desiring, melting with tenderness’, so that the present agony mirrors the past yearning sound for sound. Uḷ nīr aṟuka is an optative, ‘may the water within be cut off’, a mock-curse on the eyes that ‘longed and saw him’ (vēṇṭi avark kaṇṭa kaṇ). Commentators differ on whether the curse is sleeplessness plus tears (Mu. Varadarasanar) or an address directly to the eyes (Kalaignar: ‘O eyes… suffer!’); Puliyur Kesikan reads viḻaintu as part of the past delight. Pope: ‘Aching, aching, let those exhaust their stream, / That melting, melting, that day gazed on him.’ No variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பேணாது பெட்டார் உளர்மன்னோ மற்றவர்க்
காணாது அமைவில கண்.
transliteration:
Paenaadhu pettaar ularmanno matravark
kaanaadhu amaivila kan.
current_meaning: There is one who loved me without truly caring for me; and yet my eyes cannot rest without seeing him.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever had a friend who said they liked you but didn’t really act like it, and still you kept looking for them on the playground? The lady feels like that. She knows he isn’t caring for her the way he should, but her eyes still keep searching for him.
university_explanation: Pēṇātu peṭṭār, ‘one who desired (me) without cherishing (me)’, sets peṭṭal (to desire, to love) against pēṇutal (to care for, to tend); uḷar maṉṉō, ‘there is indeed such a one’, carries a sigh of reproach. Avark kāṇātu amaivila kaṇ: ‘without seeing him, the eyes do not settle’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss the first line as ‘loved in word only, not in heart’, and Pope’s prose follows this: ‘He is indeed here who loved me with his lips but not with his heart but mine eyes suffer from not seeing him’, while his verse reads ‘Who loved me once, unloving now doth here remain’. Commentators thus differ on whether the husband is physically near but emotionally absent or simply away; the eyes’ restlessness is the same either way. No variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா ஆயிடை
ஆரஞர் உற்றன கண்.
transliteration:
Vaaraakkaal thunjaa varindhunjaa aayidai
aaranjar utrana kan.
current_meaning: When he does not come, my eyes do not sleep; when he comes, they still do not sleep; caught between the two, they suffer unbearable pain.
elementary_explanation: Imagine waiting up for someone you love to come home: you can’t sleep because you’re waiting. Then they come, and you still can’t sleep because you’re so happy, and maybe worried they’ll leave again. The lady’s eyes get no rest either way.
university_explanation: The couplet is a neat antithesis: vārākkāl tuñcā, ‘when he does not come, they do not sleep’, and varin tuñcā, ‘if he comes, they do not sleep’; āyiṭai, ‘between these two’, the eyes uṟṟaṉa ār añar, ‘have met with grievous pain’. Commentators supply the reasons: in absence the eyes watch for his coming, and in presence they fear his departure (Solomon Pappaiah, Puliyur Kesikan: pirivu añci, ‘dreading separation’). Kalaignar generalises it to ‘such suffering can only belong to lovers’ eyes’. Pope: ‘When he comes not, all slumber flies; no sleep when he is there; / Thus every way my eyes have troubles hard to bear.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மறைபெறல் ஊரார்க்கு அரிதன்றால் எம்போல்
அறைபறை கண்ணார் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Maraiperal ooraarkku aridhandraal empoal
araiparai kannaar agaththu.
current_meaning: It is no hard thing for the townsfolk to learn the secret in the hearts of women like me, whose eyes announce it like a beaten drum.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever tried to keep a secret, but your face gave it away? Maybe you were trying not to smile about a surprise, and everyone could tell! The lady says her red, teary eyes are like a loud drum telling the whole town, ‘She misses him!’
university_explanation: Maṟai (மறை) is ‘secret’ and aṟai paṟai (அறைபறை) ‘a drum that is beaten’, the town crier’s drum used for public proclamations; kaṇṇār akattu, ‘in the hearts of those whose eyes (are such drums)’. The couplet closes the chapter by turning from the eyes’ private suffering to their public betrayal: whatever the heroine hides, her tear-stained eyes broadcast it. It also links back to chapter 115 (alar, village gossip). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read the drum as the weeping that reveals the inner state; Pope: ‘It is not hard for all the town the knowledge to obtain, / When eyes, as mine, like beaten tambours, make the mystery plain.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நயந்தவர்க்கு நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன் பசந்தவென்
பண்பியார்க்கு உரைக்கோ பிற.
transliteration:
nayandhavarkku nalkaamai naerndhaen pasandhaven
panpiyaarkku uraikko pira
current_meaning: I myself agreed to let my loving husband go away; now that my body has turned pale with longing, to whom else can I complain about it?
elementary_explanation: Imagine you told your best friend, ‘It’s okay, go on the trip without me,’ and then you missed them so much you felt sick. You can’t really complain to anyone, because you said yes! The wife in this couplet feels exactly that way.
university_explanation: Chapter 119 of the karpiyal (married love) section turns on pasalai or pasappu (பசலை / பசப்பு), the sallow, pallid tint that classical Tamil poetics treats as the visible sign of a wife’s grief in separation; both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net title the chapter பசப்புறு பருவரல் (pasappuṟu paruvaral, ‘the distress of having become pallid’), while this edition’s chapter list spells it பசப்பறு. In this opening couplet the heroine admits that she nērntēn (நேர்ந்தேன், ‘consented’) to nalkāmai (நல்காமை, literally ‘not showing grace’, which the modern commentators Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss as the husband’s separation); having agreed, she has forfeited the right to complain, hence yārkku uraikkō piṟa, ‘to whom else shall I tell it?’. In the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar the chapter is voiced by the heroine to her confidante (tōḻi), and the irony of complaining while saying one cannot complain is the point. Pope renders: ‘I willed my lover absent should remain; / Of pining’s sickly hue to whom shall I complain?’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அவர்தந்தார் என்னும் தகையால் இவர்தந்தென்
மேனிமேல் ஊரும் பசப்பு.
transliteration:
avardhandhaar ennum thakaiyaal ivardhandhaen
maenimael oorum pasappu
current_meaning: Proud that it was given to me by him, this pallor climbs all over my body and spreads as if it owned it.
elementary_explanation: Think of a sticker your favourite person gave you: you might put it everywhere, proud of it because of who gave it. The wife says the pale colour on her skin acts like that sticker. It spreads all over her, proud because her husband ‘gave’ it to her by going away.
university_explanation: The heroine personifies pasappu (பசப்பு) as a proud guest: avar tantār ennum takaiyāl, ‘with the dignity of “he gave it”’, it ivarntu (இவர்ந்து, ‘mounting, climbing’) and ūrum (ஊரும், ‘creeps, spreads, rides’) over her mēni (மேனி, body, complexion). Takai here is ‘worth, pride’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both render the pallor as spreading ‘with pride’ (பெருமிதம்) because the lover caused it. Pope’s rendering takes ūrum in the sense of riding: ‘“He gave”: this sickly hue thus proudly speaks, / Then climbs, and all my frame its chariot makes.’ The conceit, that even the affliction is precious because it comes from him, is characteristic of the karpiyal chapters and of the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar, in which the wife cannot fully resent what her husband’s absence has given her. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சாயலும் நாணும் அவர்கொண்டார் கைம்மாறா
நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து.
transliteration:
saayalum naanum avarkondaar kaimmaaraa
noayum pasalaiyum thandhu
current_meaning: He took away my beauty and my modesty, and in exchange he gave me love-sickness and this pallor.
elementary_explanation: Imagine trading your shiny new toy for a broken one and a bad cold. Not a fair swap! The wife jokes sadly that her husband made a swap like that: he took her bright looks and her shyness, and left her with sadness and a pale face.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on the language of exchange: kaimmāṟā (கைம்மாறா, ‘as a return, in exchange’) the husband took (koṇṭār) her sāyal (சாயல், grace, soft beauty) and nāṇ (நாண், modesty, the sense of shame proper to a woman in Sangam poetics) and gave (tantu) nōy (நோய், the disease of love) and pasalai (பசலை). The loss of nāṇ ties back to chapter 114 (நாணுத் துறவுரைத்தல், ‘declaring the abandonment of modesty’). Solomon Pappaiah reads the exchange as happening at the very moment of parting; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the bare trade. Pope renders: ‘Of comeliness and shame he me bereft, / While pain and sickly hue, in recompense, he left.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் உரைப்பது அவர்திறமால்
கள்ளம் பிறவோ பசப்பு.
transliteration:
ulluvan manyaan uraippadhu avardhiramaal
kallam piravo pasappu
current_meaning: I think only of him, and all I speak of is his goodness; yet the pallor has come all the same. Is it not a trick?
elementary_explanation: Imagine you did all your homework and studied hard, and still got a bad mark. You’d say, ‘That’s not fair, I did everything right!’ The wife says the same: she thinks about her husband all day and only says good things about him, yet the sad pale colour still came. It feels like a trick.
university_explanation: The heroine protests that she has kept faith in thought and speech: uḷḷuvan maṉ yāṉ (உள்ளுவன் மன் யான், ‘I do indeed think of him’), uraippatu avar tiṟam (உரைப்பது அவர் திறம், ‘what I speak is his worth’), so the pallor must be kaḷḷam (கள்ளம், ‘deceit, theft’) or come by some other way (piṟavō). The implied logic, made explicit by the commentators, is that constant remembrance should keep the absent one ‘present’, so the pallor of separation has no right to appear. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render kaḷḷam as vañcaṉai/vañcakam (treachery); Kalaignar instead asks how the pallor came ‘without my knowing or by some other path’. Pope: ‘I meditate his words, his worth is theme of all I say, / This sickly hue is false that would my trust betray.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உவக்காண்எம் காதலர் செல்வார் இவக்காண்என்
மேனி பசப்பூர் வது.
transliteration:
uvakkaan-em kaadhalar selvaar ivakkaan-en
maeni pasappoor vadhu
current_meaning: Look there, my lover is walking away; and look here, the pallor is already creeping over my body.
elementary_explanation: Picture an ice cream on a hot day: the moment you take it out of the freezer, it starts to melt. The wife says that the moment her husband started walking away, before he was even out of sight, her face started going pale.
university_explanation: The couplet’s force lies in two deictic phrases: uvakkāṇ (உவக்காண், ‘see, over there’, using the mid-distance demonstrative u-) and ivakkāṇ (இவக்காண், ‘see, right here’), setting the departing husband and the arriving pallor side by side as simultaneous events; pasappu ūrvatu (பசப்பு ஊர்வது) is ‘the creeping of pallor’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan keep the present tense (‘there he goes; here it spreads’), whereas Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a memory of how, even in earlier partings, the pallor came the instant he left, so that the present absence must be worse. Pope’s version, ‘My lover there went forth to roam; / This pallor of my frame usurps his place at home’, adds the idea of the pallor taking his place. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
விளக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் இருளேபோல் கொண்கன்
முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் பசப்பு.
transliteration:
vilakkatram paarkkum irulepoal kon-kan
muyakkatram paarkkum pasappu
current_meaning: Just as darkness waits for the lamp to fail, the pallor waits for the moment my husband’s embrace loosens.
elementary_explanation: When you blow out a candle, the dark rushes in right away, as if it had been waiting just outside the light. The wife says the sad pale colour is like that dark: it waits, and as soon as her husband’s hug ends, it rushes in.
university_explanation: A celebrated simile: viḷakku aṟṟam pārkkum iruḷ (விளக்கு அற்றம் பார்க்கும் இருள், ‘darkness that watches for the lamp’s lapse’) is set against koṇkaṉ muyakku aṟṟam pārkkum pasappu (‘pallor that watches for the lapse of my husband’s embrace’). Aṟṟam (அற்றம்) means a gap, failing or unguarded moment; pārkkum is ‘watches for, lies in wait’. Koṇkaṉ (கொண்கன்) is a classical word for husband, traditionally associated with the seashore (neytal) landscape. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the embrace’s aṟṟam as its slackening, Solomon Pappaiah as its loosening, and Kalaignar as the moment the tight hold relaxes. Pope: ‘As darkness waits till lamp expires, to fill the place, / This pallor waits till I enjoy no more my lord’s embrace.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the transliteration kon-kan follows ytamizh.

tamil:
புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன் புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில்
அள்ளிக்கொள் வற்றே பசப்பு.
transliteration:
pullik kidandhen pudaipeyarndhaen avvalavil
allikkol vatre pasappu
current_meaning: I lay held close in his arms; I merely turned aside a little, and in that instant the pallor swept over me as if scooping me up.
elementary_explanation: You know how a snowman starts melting the second the sun comes out? The wife says she was cuddled up safe and happy, turned over for just a moment, and in that tiny moment the sad pale colour grabbed her, like a big scoop.
university_explanation: The couplet heightens the previous one by shrinking the interval to almost nothing: pullik kiṭantēṉ (புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன், ‘I lay embracing’), puṭai peyarntēṉ (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன், ‘I shifted to one side’), avvaḷavil (‘in just that much’), the pallor aḷḷik koḷvaṟṟē (அள்ளிக்கொள்வற்றே, ‘was like something scooped up in handfuls’, i.e. it came in a rush). Solomon Pappaiah frames it as a recollection of an earlier occasion, making the point a fortiori for the present long absence, while Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan keep it as a vivid present. Pope: ‘I lay in his embrace, I turned unwittingly; / Forthwith this hue, as you might grasp it, came on me.’ The treatment is tasteful and hyperbolic, the conventional rhetoric of the heroine’s extreme sensitivity. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பசந்தாள் இவள்என்பது அல்லால் இவளைத்
துறந்தார் அவர்என்பார் இல்.
transliteration:
pasandhaal ival-enpadhu allaal ivalaith
thurandhaar avar-enpaar il
current_meaning: People only say, ‘She has turned pale’; no one says, ‘He has left her.’
elementary_explanation: Imagine your friend broke your toy, and everyone said, ‘Why is that toy broken? You must be careless!’ but nobody said, ‘Your friend broke it.’ That feels unfair. The wife feels the same: everybody notices her pale face, but nobody says it’s because her husband went away.
university_explanation: A couplet about public opinion (alar, the village gossip that runs through the Kamattuppal): people say pasantāḷ ivaḷ (பசந்தாள் இவள், ‘she has grown pale’), but none says tuṟantār avar (துறந்தார் அவர், ‘he has abandoned her’). Tuṟa- is the same root as tuṟavu, ‘renunciation, forsaking’, giving the complaint a sharp edge. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the first clause as blame (பழி) directed at the woman for showing her grief, while the man’s departure, the real cause, escapes comment. Pope: ‘On me, because I pine, they cast a slur; / But no one says, “He first deserted her.”’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பசக்கமன் பட்டாங்கென் மேனி நயப்பித்தார்
நன்னிலையர் ஆவர் எனின்.
transliteration:
pasakkaman pattaangen maeni nayappiththaar
nannilaiyar aavar enin
current_meaning: If he who sweetly persuaded me to let him go is himself well and in good standing, then let my body turn as pale as it will.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your big brother goes away to camp and you miss him so much you feel sad. But then you think, ‘As long as he’s having fun and is safe, I don’t mind being a bit sad.’ That is what the wife says: if her husband is doing well, she doesn’t mind the pale colour.
university_explanation: Here the heroine turns from complaint to self-sacrifice: pasakka maṉ (பசக்க மன், ‘let it grow pale indeed’), paṭṭāṅku (பட்டாங்கு, ‘as it actually is, to its full measure’) eṉ mēṉi, if nayappittār (நயப்பித்தார், ‘he who made me consent by sweet persuasion’, from nayam, pleasantness) is nannilaiyar (நன்னிலையர், ‘of good standing’). Commentators divide on nannilaiyar: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as ‘good, blameless’, so the verse is half ironic, while Kalaignar reads ‘is well, prospers’, making it a wish for his welfare; the Pope translation (‘in good estate remain’) supports the latter, and the alternative rendering on ytamizh, ‘if he is clear of guilt’, supports the former. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பசப்பெனப் பேர்பெறுதல் நன்றே நயப்பித்தார்
நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்.
transliteration:
pasappenap paerperudhal nandre nayappiththaar
nalkaamai thootraar enin
current_meaning: It is fine for me to be known as ‘the pale one’, so long as people do not slander him who persuaded me to let him go for his unkindness.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your friend forgot your birthday, and you felt sad. If people started saying mean things about your friend, you might say, ‘It’s okay, just call me the sad one, but please don’t be mean to my friend.’ That’s what the wife says: call me pale, but don’t blame him.
university_explanation: The chapter closes on the heroine’s protectiveness: pasappu eṉap pēr peṟutal naṉṟē (பசப்பெனப் பேர்பெறுதல் நன்றே, ‘it is good to get the name of pallor’), if people tūṟṟār (தூற்றார், ‘do not slander, broadcast in blame’) the nalkāmai (நல்காமை, ‘lack of grace, unkindness’) of nayappittār (‘him who won my consent’). The verse answers 1188: there she resented that people blamed her and not him; here she would rather keep the blame herself than have his name spoiled, a turn the commentators read as the ideal of the karpu (chaste, loyal) wife. Solomon Pappaiah takes the people as those who would otherwise abuse him for not returning; Kalaignar as those who would call him loveless. Pope: ‘’Tis well, though men deride me for my sickly hue of pain; / If they from calling him unkind, who won my love, refrain.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the opening verb nalkāmai echoes Kural 1181, framing the chapter.

tamil:
தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர் பெற்றாரே
காமத்துக் காழில் கனி.
transliteration:
Thaamveezhvaar thamveezhap petravar petraare
kaamaththuk kaazhil kani.
current_meaning: Those who are loved in return by the very one they love have won love’s best prize: a fruit with no hard stone inside, all sweetness.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you save half your sandwich for your best friend, and your best friend has saved half of theirs for you. That happy feeling of sharing both ways is like biting into a fruit with no pit at all: nothing hard to spoil it.
university_explanation: Chapter 120, tanippaṭar mikuti (‘the excess of solitary suffering’), belongs to the karpiyal (married love) sequence on separation; in the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar the heroine, left alone, fears that her longing is not matched by her absent husband’s and speaks to her confidante (tōḻi). The chapter opens by defining what she lacks: tām vīḻvār tam vīḻap peṟṟavar, those whom the ones they desire (vīḻ, ‘to desire, fall for’) desire in turn. Kāḻ il kaṉi is ‘a fruit without a stone (kāḻ)’, i.e. pleasure without any hard residue of pain; Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss it as the seedless fruit that is the yield (payaṉ) of married love. Pope renders: ‘The bliss to be beloved by those they love who gains, / Of love the stoneless, luscious fruit obtains.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்றால் வீழ்வார்க்கு
வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி.
transliteration:
Vaazhvaarkku vaanam payandhatraal veezhvaarkku
veezhvaar alikkum ali.
current_meaning: The tenderness a lover shows to the one who loves him is like rain from the sky to those whose life depends on it.
elementary_explanation: Think of a thirsty garden in summer. When the rain finally comes, every leaf perks up. When someone you love is kind to you, your heart perks up the same way.
university_explanation: The couplet sets the beloved’s aḷi (grace, tender kindness) beside the rain that the sky (vāṉam) yields (payanta) to living beings (vāḻvār), echoing the Kural’s own chapter on rain (vāṉ ciṟappu, ch. 2). Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators take vāḻvār as ‘those who live by it’ and insist on timeliness: Pappaiah stresses rain at the proper season, and Kalaignar reads it as lovers meeting at the right time. The point in this chapter is implicit contrast: the heroine is the parched field to whom no such rain is coming. Pope: ‘As heaven on living men showers blessings from above, / Is tender grace by lovers shown to those they love.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வீழுநர் வீழப் படுவார்க்கு அமையுமே
வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Veezhunar veezhap paduvaarkku amaiyume
vaazhunam ennum serukku.
current_meaning: Only a woman truly loved by the one she loves can carry the proud confidence that says, ‘We shall live happily yet,’ even while he is away.
elementary_explanation: If your mom goes on a trip and you know she loves you and will come back, you can wait bravely and even smile. Knowing you are loved makes waiting easier.
university_explanation: Vīḻunar vīḻappaṭuvār is ‘those who are desired by the ones who desire them’; for such women alone amaiyumē (it is fitting) to hold the ceruukku (pride, proud confidence) of saying vāḻunam, ‘we shall live (in joy).’ In the separation context Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read the pride as forward-looking: despite present parting, the loved wife can be sure that reunion and happiness will come; Pappaiah adds ‘by the certainty that he will soon return.’ The heroine’s unspoken complaint is that she cannot claim this pride. Pope: ‘Who love and are beloved to them alone / Belongs the boast, “We’ve made life’s very joys our own.”’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வீழப் படுவார் கெழீஇயிலர் தாம்வீழ்வார்
வீழப் படாஅர் எனின்.
transliteration:
Veezhap paduvaar kezhee-iyilar thaamveezhvaar
veezhap pataa-ar enin.
current_meaning: Even a woman admired by everyone is truly unfortunate if the one she loves does not love her back.
elementary_explanation: Imagine everyone at school likes your drawing, but the one person you made it for doesn’t care about it. All the other praise wouldn’t feel like enough. The Kural says love works like that.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a contrast within the same verb: vīḻappaṭuvār, ‘those who are desired’ (by others, or by the world), are kezhīiyilar, ‘not endowed (with good fortune)’, if they are vīḻappaṭār, ‘not desired’, by tām vīḻvār, ‘those whom they themselves desire.’ Parimelazhagar’s line, followed by Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, glosses kezhīiyilar as lacking nalviṉai (the fruit of past merit); Pappaiah sharpens it to being under tīviṉai, while Kalaignar instead reads the lover as lacking the friendly feeling. Pope: ‘Those well-beloved will luckless prove, / Unless beloved by those they love.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both with the alapeṭai spelling படாஅர்.

tamil:
நாம்காதல் கொண்டார் நமக்கெவன் செய்பவோ
தாம்காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Naamkaadhal kondaar namakkevan seypavo
thaamkaadhal kollaak kadai.
current_meaning: If the one I love does not love me in return, what good can he possibly do me?
elementary_explanation: If you keep waving at someone across the playground and they never wave back, the waving can’t make you happy. Love needs someone answering from the other side.
university_explanation: The question form nam(a)kku evaṉ ceypavō, ‘what will they do for us?’, is rhetorical: the heroine admits that her own love (nām kātal koṇṭār, ‘the one we have taken love for’) can bring her nothing if tām kātal koḷḷā kaṭai, ‘when he does not take love (for us).’ Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar, makes the implied answer ‘no good at all’; Pappaiah and Kalaignar render ‘what joy will he give?’ The polite plural (koṇṭār, ceypa) keeps the husband at a distance even as she complains. Pope: ‘From him I love to me what gain can be, / Unless, as I love him, he loveth me?’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஒருதலையான் இன்னாது காமம்காப் போல
இருதலை யானும் இனிது.
transliteration:
Orudhalaiyaan innaadhu kaamamkaap pola
irudhalai yaanum inidhu.
current_meaning: Love that sits at one end only is painful; like the load on a carrying pole, it is sweet only when it is balanced at both ends.
elementary_explanation: Have you tried carrying two buckets on a stick across your shoulders? With one bucket it tips and hurts, but with one on each side it’s easy. Love is the same: it feels good only when both people carry it.
university_explanation: This is the Kural’s most famous image for mutual love. Kā is the kāvaṭi or shoulder-pole carried with a load at each end; orutalai (‘one end’) and irutalai (‘two ends’) give Tamil the still-current phrase orutalaik kātal for one-sided love. Kāmam orutalaiyāṉ iṉṉātu, ‘love on one end is painful’, irutalaiyāṉum iṉitu, ‘on both ends it is sweet.’ Parimelazhagar takes the kā simile as governing both halves; Kalaignar spells out that the pole’s two sides must be equally weighted, as love must bloom in both man and woman. Pope: ‘Love on one side is bad; like balanced load / By porter borne, love on both sides is good.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பருவரலும் பைதலும் காணான்கொல் காமன்
ஒருவர்கண் நின்றொழுகு வான்.
transliteration:
Paruvaralum paidhalum kaanaankol kaaman
oruvar-kan nindrozhuku vaan.
current_meaning: The god of love works on one side only; does he not see the pain and sorrow he leaves in me?
elementary_explanation: It’s like a game where only one team is allowed to play and the other just has to watch. It doesn’t seem fair. Here the girl feels that love has been fair to her husband but very unfair to her.
university_explanation: Kāmaṉ is the god of love (Sanskrit Kāma, Manmatha), whose flower-arrows awaken desire. The heroine complains that he oruvarkaṇ niṉṟu oḻukuvāṉ, ‘stays and works upon one person only’, i.e. on her, not on her absent husband, and asks whether he does not see her paruvaral (distress) and paital (sorrow). Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, takes the complaint as against Kāma’s partiality; Pappaiah and Kalaignar connect paital with the pallor (pacalai) of the previous chapter. Pope: ‘While Kaman rushes straight at me alone, / Is all my pain and wasting grief unknown?’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வீழ்வாரின் இன்சொல் பெறாஅது உலகத்து
வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்.
transliteration:
Veezhvaarin insol peraaadhu ulakaththu
vaazhvaarin vankanaar il.
current_meaning: No one in the world is as hard-hearted, or as brave, as a woman who goes on living without even one kind word from the one she loves.
elementary_explanation: Imagine waiting every day for a letter from someone you love, and none ever comes, yet you keep getting up and going to school. That takes a very strong heart. The Kural says it is almost too strong.
university_explanation: Vaṉkaṇār means both ‘the hard-hearted, cruel’ and ‘the brave, enduring’, and the couplet exploits the ambiguity with self-irony: the heroine says that those who go on living in the world (ulakattu vāḻvār) without receiving (peṟāatu) even a sweet word (iṉcol) from their beloved (vīḻvār) are the most vaṉkaṇ of all. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read vaṉkaṇmai as the stony endurance of separation; Pappaiah’s ‘no one is more cruel’ and Kalaignar’s ‘no one has so stony a heart’ stress self-reproach, while Pope chooses the heroic sense: ‘Who hear from lover’s lips no pleasant word from day to day, / Yet in the world live out their life,- no braver souls than they!’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நசைஇயார் நல்கார் எனினும் அவர்மாட்டு
இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு.
transliteration:
Nasai-iyaar nalkaar eninum avarmaattu
isaiyum iniya sevikku.
current_meaning: Even if the one I long for shows me no kindness, every word about him, even his very name, is still sweet to my ears.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes when you miss someone, just hearing their name makes you smile, even if they haven’t called you. The girl in this couplet feels that way: anything about him sounds like music.
university_explanation: Nacaiiyār (with alapeṭai) is ‘the one longed for’; nalkār eṉiṉum, ‘even though he grants no grace’; avar māṭṭu icaiyum, ‘even what is heard of / from him’, is iṉiya cevikku, ‘sweet to the ear.’ The word icai is read two ways: as ‘fame, praise’ (Parimelazhagar’s line, followed by Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar: hearing others praise him is honey to her), or as ‘word, sound’ (Pappaiah: any word from him is sweet). Pope follows the second: ‘Though he my heart desires no grace accords to me, / Yet every accent of his voice is melody.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய் கடலைச்
செறாஅஅய் வாழிய நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Uraaarkku urunoi uraippaai kadalaich
cheraaaai vaazhiya nenju.
current_meaning: Bless you, my heart! You keep telling your great pain to one who cares nothing for you; you might as well try to fill up the sea.
elementary_explanation: Imagine trying to fill the ocean with a bucket. No matter how much you pour, it never fills. The girl tells her own heart that telling her sadness to someone who doesn’t care is just like that.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with an apostrophe to the heart (neñcu), a figure that the next chapters develop. Uṟāarkku is ‘to one who is not attached (to you)’, uṟunōy ‘the great affliction (you suffer)’, uraippāy ‘you who tell’; kaṭalaic ceṟāaay is read as an ironic imperative, ‘(go and) fill up the sea!’ Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar, is comparative: filling the sea would be easier than winning comfort from the indifferent. Vāḻiya, ‘may you live / bless you’, is half-pitying, half-mocking. Pope: ‘Tell him thy pain that loves not thee? / Farewell, my soul, fill up the sea!’, while his prose gloss reads the sea as her own sea of sorrow. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both with the triple alapeṭai செறாஅஅய்.
